Recommendation ( Para 7.3)
 
System of Sub-Contracting Business Pattern
           
            The Committee understands the compelling circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of sub-
contracting business pattern but it is also an open secret that sub-contracting gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the Company itself.  The Committee is of the view that VRS offer by HSCL to its employees would take
care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of productive age profile and willing to undertake work/assignment
from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give
larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of
sub-contracting is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees, sooner than later.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the separation of manpower in accordance with the provision of the Restructuring Proposal and
MOU with Ministry of Steel,  HSCL will be left out with only about 1000 employees on its rolls.  In such
circumstances, HSCL’s function will  be of supervisory nature only.  However, execution of contracts will be carried
out as per the approved procedures of the Company.  Adequate steps will be taken to optimize margins and use of
departmental inputs.
 
Further recommendation
 
            The Committee feels that  entrusting  HSCL merely  with the supervisory role  and continuing  with   the system
of sub-contracting would not be  a  sustainable proposition  for the Company.   There is no need   for making a mini
Ministry   with in the  Ministry  of Steel .  The Ministry of Steel is already playing the  supervisory role  over the steel
PSUs,   therefore,  steel PSUs should  do the actual  work, the Committee feels .  The Committee,  therefore,   reiterates  
that   direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give  larger  margin to HSCL and thus opening  scope for
profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of sub-contracting is  replaced  by direct involvement
of HSCL employees, sooner than later.

Recommendation ( Para 9.4)
           
Preferential treatment to HSCL in procurement of work order from SAIL and other Government’s Department
 
The Committee is of the view that HSCL deserves a better deal  in SAIL with Government mediation,
therefore the Committee recommends that all the projects as well as AMR and operational jobs, within the
execution capacity of HSCL, should be offered on nomination on priority basis to HSCL.  This would enable the
Company to utilise its infrastructure, set up over the years at SAIL plants and meet the expenses of the
Company.  Award procedure of SAIL should be relaxed suitably for preferential treatment to HSCL.  The
Company may have long term arrangement/understanding with SAIL on the basis of quantum of job assured for
award.  The Committee further recommends that a certain portion of the construction jobs in the infrastructural
sector be assigned to HSCL  on nomination basis, at least during the initial years of planned revival.  Purchase
preference to PSUs should be strictly adhered to.  Presently the PSUs/Government Department are not
uniformly following the system.  The dismal balance sheets of the Company, for several years now have made
customers apprehensive in pre-qualifying HSCL for their prospects.  Judging the merit of the situation
respective Administrative Ministries may issue necessary directives not to disqualify   HSCL for quoting, based
on the financial performance of last few years.  HSCL should be granted relaxation in registration formalities
with Government Departments for taking up work.  HSCL shouldbe exempted from submitting EMD for taking
up work with Government departments and PSUs.    HSCL’s experience in construction of roads in the
integrated steel plants should be considered as qualifying  criterion for High way work and matter may be taken
up with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highway.

of work on nomination basis.  The Ministry of Steel has been actively taking up the case of HSCL in the award of works
with other Central Government Departments and Ministries as also with State Governments.
 
Further recommendation
 
SAIL  giving  work order to HSCL

Recommendation  (Para 13.3 )
 
Full and final settlement
 
The Committee recommends that HSCL management should not delay in the settlement of full and final
accounts  for all HSCL employees who have opted for VRS.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Government has been informed by HSCL that in all cases (8177 cases) of employees separated under VRS
ex-gratia has been settled in full.  In 26 cases leave encashment and in 6 cases gratuity payment is still pending. 
However in 6862 cases transportation dues are pending as these are under scrutiny in view of certain audit objections
raised in the matter.  Arrears remain to be settled on account of outstanding wages and salaries for these employees. 
These remain unpaid on account of lack of financial resources on the part of the Company.  While releasing financial
assistance of Rs.89.44 crore, in the month of March, 2002, Government advised, as an interim measure, the Company to
first settle the dues of retired and separated employees based on 4
th Pay Commission pay scales.  Balance dues of the
retired/separated employees, on account of unpaid wages and salaries will be cleared after Ministry of Finance approves
a proposal made by the Ministry of Steel for releasing financial assistance for a further amount of Rs.133 crore.  The
proposal has not yet been examined by the Ministry of Finance as the Ministry of Steel is still in the process of getting
legal opinion about the implementation of the recommendations of the 5
th Pay Commission by the Company.  It may be
noted that the Ministry of Finance has not been agreeing to release financial assistance to take care of liability of the
Company arising out of implementation of the 5th Pay Commission  recommendations as the same was implemented by
the Company without the approval of the competent authority.
 
Further recommendation
 
The Committee is of the view that  HSCL management , while making  settlement  of full and final   accounts
for all HSCL employees who have opted for VRS,  should  differentiate the cases of pending settlement due to audit
objection and arrears to be settled on account of outstanding wages and salaries for these  employees due to  lack of 
financial resources on the part of  the Company.  The HSCL management and the Ministry of Steel  should  expedite  
the process of making settlement  of outstanding  wages and salaries  with the sanction of the    revival package.   The
Committee further recommends that  as soon as  the legal  wrangles    regarding   the implementation  of the 
recommendation   of the Fifth Pay Commission  gets  solved  and  the Ministry of Finance    releases  financial
assistance to HSCL ,    balance dues  of the retired /separated employees should be made .
 
Recommendation ( Para 16.3 )
 
Non-plan assistance of Rs.125.17 crore
 
            The Committee however, is of the view that the Ministry of Finance should consider the proposal of the Ministry
of Steel for grant of non-plan assistance of   Rs.125.17 crore to enable HSCL to discharge its liabilities towards payment
of arrears of wages and salaries of its employees.  The Committee is of the opinion that once a comprehensive package
for revival of HSCL is sanctioned in one go the Company would be able to come out of red.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Ministry of Steel has been pursuing the matter relating to grant of full financial assistance to the Company
to enable it to discharge its entire liability towards payment of wages and salaries to its employees.  As mentioned

the entire financial assistance package.  The Ministry of Steel is therefore, examining the implementation of the 5 th Pay
Commission recommendations in the Company, in consultation with Ministry of Law.  It appears that the Company had

            The  Committee   observes that    the prima-facie  stand of the Ministry of Steel , on the issue    of
implementation    of 5 th Pay Commission recommendation, that the Company  had implemented the 5 th Pay
Commission recommendations without the  approval of the  competent  authority but, ( as per the apprehension of the
Ministry of Steel)  in pursuance   of a Supreme Court order ,  as also in pursuance of  DPE’s  OMs,  constitute  the
vicious circle.  The  question arises  whether  on the issue,  the judicious  decision was  taken by the  competent
authority  but  on pursuance of  implementing the supreme court order or    simply the laid down procedure was not
followed.   The Committee is of the opinion that  the Ministry of Steel should have come forward immediately after 
passing  of Supreme Court Order for implementation  of its order as per  laid down  procedure.    Now  sitting over the  
issue  would   solve no purpose.  Therefore,  the Committee recommends that the   Ministry of  Steel should  form  the
final opinion without delay, and  if  required     may give  ex-post  facto   approval  to the decision   to implement the 5
th
Pay   Commission  and formulate  comprehensive  for revival   of HSCL    and forward the same   to the Ministry of 
Finance for the Grant of  full   financial  assistance   to liquidate the entire outstanding liability of the Company on

Departments   as also with the State Governments,  the Committee  reiterates  that   HSCL  should continue to get   the

assistance to HSCL ,    balance dues  of the retired /separated employees ,would be made .

Non-plan assistance of Rs.125.17 crore
 
            The Committee   observes that    the prima-facie  stands of the Ministry of Steel , on the issue    of
implementation    of 5th Pay Commission recommendation, that the Company  had implemented the 5th pay
Commission recommendations without the  approval of the  competent  authority but, ( as per the apprehension of the
Ministry of Steel)  in pursuance   of a Supreme Court order ,  as also in pursuance of  DPE’s  OMs,  constitute  the

Limited (SOVL), who are the Strategic Partners (SP).The SHA  stipulates the terms and conditions for managing the
affairs of disinvested HZL including reconstitution of the Board of Directors. In terms of this Agreement the SP has

of the company. The Government shall have the right to nominate five directors and will be called “Government
Nominee Director” and all will be non-executive directors of the company. The Chairperson of the Board of
disinvested HZL would be from the Government Nominee Directors till such time as the SP holds less than 51 per
cent of the share capital.

CHAPTER – V
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
1.            Management of Company Affairs
 
            The Committee notes the composition of the Board of  Directors of the Company which is expected to manage
the affairs of the company in accordance with the Articles of Association of the Company and The Companies Act
1956.  the Committee expects that new managements would ensure that no deviation is made in this regard.
 
2.         Special consent required from the Government
 
            The Committee notes the provisions identified in Schedule 4.5 of Shareholders Agreement (SHA) where special
consent is required from the Government for transecting the business pertaining of those items. The Committee
recommends that “Government Nominee Director” would actively participate in the meeting of Board of Director of the
Company and would keep the Government well informed the decision reached in the meeting.   The Governments
Nominee Director need to be vigilant and epitome of ensuring responsive and responsible management of affairs in the
Company.
 
3.            Adequate job opportunities for SC/ST physically handicapped persons

            The Committee is happy to note that the strategic partners recognizes that Government in relation to its
employment policies follows certain principles for the benefit of the members of the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes,
physically handicapped persons and other socially disadvantaged categories of the society.  The SP shall use its best
efforts to cause the Company to provide adequate job opportunities for such persons.  Further, in the event of any
reduction in the strength of the Employees of the Company, the SP shall use its best efforts to ensure that the physically
handicapped persons, Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes are retrenched at the end.  The Committee hopes that the new
management would ensure the implementation of the provision inwards and deeds.
 
4.            Efficiency Vs Human Relation Approach
 
            The Committee is of the view that the new management would take every care for optimum utilization of
manpower by adopting the principle of placing a right man at right place in right time in such a way that company
affairs are managed in the efficient and effective manners and keeping in view endowment of human values and ethics.
 
5.            Keeping track with changing economic scenario
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that the new management should keep an eye to the changing economic
scenario at the national and International market and reorient its mission and objectives so as to improve its physical and
financial performance.  In demand driven economy it is essential that adequate attention is being given to market
research and reorient its production plan as per the demand of the market.   New management should keep on analyzing
the strength, weaknesses, opportunities and threats     of the company and chalked out future course of action as per the
requirement. 
 
 
6.         New management initiative for employee participation
 
            The Committee hopes that the joint consultative Committee (JCC) consist of nominees of workmen and
management would be functional in real terms and all efforts would be made for achieving organizational goals of
productivity, quality, cost management and good employee relation.
 
7.            Initiative in Inventory Management, Sales, Marketing and Finance
 
            The Committee notes that the initiative taken by the new management in the field of inventory management,
sales, marketing and finance and hopes that such initiative would lead to quick disposal of inventories, increment in
turnover and  sales and market share of HZL products and attainment of favorable financial ratios.

environmental awareness  and sustainable development objectives recommends that the new management would
continue with  its concerted efforts.

INTRODUCTION 
         I, the Chairman of  the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having 
been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Sixth Report on the Globalisation 
and capital goods industry pertaining to the Department of Public En terprises, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. 
2.      The Committee, in this context, held m eetings with various Minist ries and representatives o f
Industry Organisations on 16 th April, 8 th May, 25 th June, 12 th August and 27 th November, 2002 
respectively. 
3.      The Committee in its meeting held on 17th December, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
 
  
CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTION 
         A new trend of global integration began to emerge all over the world in 1980s. This was facilitated
by the gradual integration of the world economics, which ensured free flow of capital and goods from
one country to another country. Foreign capital is now freely available to finance the large infrastructure
projects. Acceptance of WTO regime  by most of the countries has si nce led to a gradual abolition o f
quantitative restrictions and reduction duties and removal of restrictions on inter-country trade. 
1.1    In our context, the Industr ial Policy of 1991 starte d the process of de-lic ensing and except 18 
industries, licensing was withdrawn. The process of de-regul ation was aimed at en larging competition 
and allowing new firms to enter the market s. The market was opened up to domestic
entrepreneurs/industrialists, which as reserved for public sector unde rtakings, and foreign capital was
provided free entry up to 51% equity in high technol ogy areas. With the adve nt of globalization, when
World Bank-aided projects started to come to country, the lifting of import control and drastic reduction 
of import duties, competition from overseas posed a proble m to the domestic capital goods industry. It
has become difficult to stay in the race for this industry in the fa ce of stiff competition from the
multinational giants. 
1.2    Despite the tremendous odds even on date, there are examples of various domestic Indian
companies in sectors like automobi les, steel, engineering, etc. in both public and private sectors that
have successfully with stood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian economy; fo r
example Maruti cars are being exported and Tata have similar plans. TISCO has been recognized as one
of the least cost steel producers in the world and companies like IRCON, BHEL and L&T have been
successfully executing contracts abroad. These com panies have mana ged to meet the stiff com petition

1.3    The Committee deliberated upon the matter and in its 36th Report observed as under:
 
         “One such company (BHEL) which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by 
the liberalization of Indian econom y. The impressive track record of  it calls for a special mention 
of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy 
Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race  despite the odds faced by  it as a result of stif f 
competition unleashed by the multina tional giants operating in its fi eld of specialization namely, 
manufacture of power plants. T hough BHEL has managed to sustain it s viability yet it is facing 
some unfair challenges. The abse nce of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational competitors 
has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This  is leading to an eve r-increasing pressure on 
its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly  upgrading its technology and has 
also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC  power projects. This 
reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve th e nation even when the odds are 
stacked against it. Therefor e, what this company requires is a li ttle help from th e Government in 
the form of suitable policy measures. In this re gard, the sub-committee draw s the attention of the 
Government to the issues of pr ice and purchase preference to BHEL, and import duty concessions 
to the foreign companies. Through  in some cases price and purchas e preference is granted to the 
PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to 
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exempti ons are precisely the 
reasons for the playing field not be ing level for domestic companies or  for that matter PSUs as the 
bids offered by foreign players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other 
words, the competition is killed well before it begins. The Committee believes that the need of the 
hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide  a level playing field to all the 
players for the sake of healthy competition. 
Committee’s Recommendations 
1.3.1   In view of the above, the Committee has come to the conclusion that the Government should take
necessary policy measures to extend 15% price and purchase preference to BHEL

policy of giving duty concessions to the foreign companies in as much as it leads to disadvantages to the
domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered view  of the committee that foreign
companies should not be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.”

2.        The Committee held meetings on 16th April, 8th May, 25th June, 12th August and 28th November,

2.1.2   The discussion could not be concluded. The convenor  requested the representatives of CII to

2.2      Meeting held on 8th May, 2002
 
2.2.1   Convenor apprised the Committee that in its last meeting held on 16 th April 2002, discussion

against World Bank/Asian Development Bank’s fina nced projects. The Convenor summarized the view
points of CII and informed the Committee that World Bank as well  as Asian Development Bank had
been financing various kinds of projects for over two decades in India. Th ere was an established

           1.     International Competitive Bidding has to be followed; 
           2.     The tenders submitted by fo reign bidders would be evalua ted without including customs

           3.     Price preference of 15% to dom estic bidders was allowed with the stipulation that it would

2.2.2   CIT further stated that the Central Board of Excise and Custom s Duty issued a notification No.

international organization. The Wo rld Bank had allowed 15% Price Pr eference to domestic bidders to

inadequate infrastructure and higher cost of finance. With zero customs duty from 6 th July 1999 fo r

reduced to zero. 
2.2.3   Secretary, Ministry of Po wer, Secretary, Department of Revenue, and Director General o f

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
3.        The amendment of Customs Notification N o. 85/99 dated 6.7.1999 was issued amending the 
earlier Notification No. 84/99 permitting imports at zero duty for projects funded by international
Organizations. With th e notification, the preference polic y under World Ba nk guideline has
automatically reduced to zero and adversely affected the domestic industry. The Committee consistently
followed up the matter and recommende d for corrective measures in its 36 th, 45th and 59th Reports and 
had five meetings with several mi nistries and public and private sect or domestic industry to resolve the
matter. The World Bank issue is not only applicable  to Public Sector Undert akings but also to capital
goods industry in general. The Committee’s objective was to utilize it for the development of the
country. 
3.1      The Committee recalls that in the meetings held on 16 th April, 8th May and 25th June, 2002, The 
Ministries/Departments had expresse d their own reservations and concer ns but ultimately they realized
that if only they put their heads together they could resolve the i ssue. The Committee appreciates the
ministries and departments for their coordinated approach. 
3.2      Since globalization, the country is facing ma ny problems but at the sa me time the country cannot
go back. We have to see how to safeguard the country’s interest – both public and private sectors. 
3.3      Now, in view of the clarificatory notification issued by the Department of  Economic Affairs,
there is no need to rescind the Notification No. 85/99 and the Comm ittee hopes that the capital goods
industry of the country would be ab le to compete with the foreign bi dders in the projects funded by

        At the outset, Convenor welcomed the Secretaries and ot her officers of the Ministries and
representatives of industries' associations. Convenor apprised the Committee that in its last meeting held
on 16th April, 2002, discussion could not be concluded and he requested CII to prepare a note regarding
imports at zero customs duty agai nst World Bank/Asian Developmen t Bank's financed projects. The
Convenor summarised the view point s of CII and informed the commit tee that World Bank as well as
Asian Development Bank had been fi nancing various kinds of projects  for over two decades in India.
There was an established procedure for inviting tenders and for evaluating them. The primary features of
the guidelines were as follows: 
        (a)   International Competitive Bidding had to be followed; 
        (b)   Evaluation of tenders submitted by foreign bidders would be evaluated without including
customs duty; and 
        (c)   Price preference of 15% to domestic bidders was allowed with the stipulation that it would be
admissible if in the total package, there was value addition of 30% or  more and the price
preference was not more than applicable customs duty. 
2.     The Central Board of Excise and Customs Duty issued a notification No. 85/99 amending an earlier
customs notification exempting cust oms duty on import of goods for  ex ecution of projects financed by
loan or grant by World Bank, Asia n Development Bank or any othe r international organisation. The
World Bank had allowed 15%  Price Preference to dom estic bidders to offset  the domestic duty/levies
such as sales tax, octrois, etc. and certain disadvant ages due to inadequate infrastructure and higher cost
of finance. With zero customs duty from 6th Jul y, 1999 for direct import by pr oject authorities, the
effect of price preference of 15% had automatically been reduced to zero. Secretary, Ministry of Power,
Secretary, Department of Revenue, Director General of Foreign Trade raised the following objections: 
        (a)    World Bank/ADB had stopped fundi ng power generation projects in  India, the rescinding o f
the aforesaid customs notification had no practical significance; 
        (b)    If the domestic price preference was restored, the project cost would go up; and 
        (c)    If domestic price preference was restored, overseas bidders would not be interested in
competing for projects funded by the World Bank/ADB. 
3.     As regard point number 1 above, CMD, BHEL, drew attention to  the press report appearing in the
Financial Express dt. 7.5.2002 where Mini ster of Power was reported to ha ve stated that Government of
India would seek financial assi stance of around $ 4 billion from ADB for implementation of various
power projects. If this wa s true, domestic companies would be pla ced at a considerable disadvantage in
the absence of domestic price pref erence. Also, the power transmissi on sector continued to avail o f 
multilateral funding for its proj ects and domestic companies incl uding BHEL were already at a
disadvantage while bidding for these projects. In view of this, it would not be correct to conclude that
the issue had no practical significance. 
        In so far as point number two was concerne d, he stated that although the project cost may have the
potential of increasing to this ex tent, this may not happen in all cas es, as this would depend upon the
pricing strategies adopted by various bidders in specific projects. However, in the absence of domestic
price preference and the consequent  disadvantage suffered by domestic industry, it was likely that more
and more contracts would be w on by the overseas bidders who w ould quote their price in foreign
currencies. These companies would te nd to adopt a different pricing stra tegy in the absence of effective
competition from capable domestic companies. Also, as these projects got executed over a time frame of
3 to 4 years and given the propensity of the Indian ru pee to depreciate (past experience showed that, on

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between stipulated
delivery period and the actual date of delivery.
3.         As per standard terms of conditions of supply contract generally also provide for force majeure clause meaning
unforeseen circumstances like legal injunctions, natural calamities, industrial action by workers etc. are reasons
attributable to the delay in supply or performance, the same is exempt from imposition of liquidated damages.
4.         The Sub-Committee-III for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises of Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry came to know about the effect of Liquidated Damages on the supplier
when it visited Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels at Visakhapatnam (a subsidiary of BYNL) on 11th July, 2000. The
workers union as well as management of BHPV informed the Committee that due to delay in deliveries, Rs. 41 crores
had been held up with different units of the company which had created cash flow problems. Later on, after visiting

5.         Thereafter,  the Committee on Industry in its 44th Report present/laid on 21st December, 2000 recommended as

5.2       The Department of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with the client PSUs for release of outstanding
amount locked-up on account of Liquidity Damages (LD) to such a possible extent, which can be released by the client

the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industry could not bear much fruit, 
Sub-Committee-III observed that these issues needed to be approached through a coordinated effort. The Committee
also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns expressed by DHI in respect of the said issue by the other
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, decided to hear both the Department of Heavy Industry and the Ministry of
Petroleum and Natural Gas to find out a probable solution.
CHAPTER–II
MEETINGS HELD WITH THE MINISTRIES AND PSUS THEREUNDER

Meeting held on 17th April, 2002

Enterprises and Petroleum and Natural Gas, and representatives of various Central PSUs. The Convenor apprised the

PSUs on the supplier PSUs for non-adherence to the delivery schedule. There had been some problems among the
PSUs. These Liduidated Damages were imposed due to delay and as a result the money had been held up and the
supplier PSUs, specially the BYNL group of companies, had been facing working capital problem.
7.2       Secretary,  Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that the engineering
industries were facing some problems as there had been no fresh investment in the economy. One of the main problems
had been the lack of working capital because the working capital limits had become irregular. The banks were not
willing to give further advance and the Government was also reluctant to issue fresh funds for the working capital. The
BYNL group of companies had a large measure of support from oil sector and the oil sector was one sector in the
economy where there had been some investment. About 50% of the turnover of these companies came from the oil
PSUs and generally oil sector PSUs also gave benefit of purchase preference to these companies. There had been delay
in execution of projects but in the recent past, these companies had assured that things had improved and some of those
delays or level of delays or the extent of delays that took place earlier, were not taking place now. The process of
disinvestments in all these companies was under way and in order to optimise the return to the Government, the

7.6.1    The Sub-Committee-III had a meeting with the Ministries of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and
Petroleum and Natural Gas where the question of Liquidity Damages (LD) came up. The Liquidity Damages is a form
of penalty, which is imposed by the client PSEs on the supplier PSEs for non-adhering to schedule delivery within the

The second is that they should continue to do well and they should not face difficulty in executing work because of lack
of finances. They were already getting the orders. In case there were any difficulties because of the lack of finances,
when both secretaries meet in the monthly meetings, they would have a discussion and see that there were no difficulties
in executing the orders. Thirdly, the Liquidating Damages question should be seen by an independent director. If this
mechanism was allowed to work for a year, it was hoped that the objective of BYNL would be achieved and time gap
reduced. When Convenor enquired whether they could do something about waiving off LDs upto March 2001,
Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas, informed that they had taken up matter to the Boards but the Boards had not
agreed to waive the Liquidated Damages. Although ONGC had argued the case in a fair manner but since ONGC had

suffered losses so they could not compound their losses by waiving the penalty on an organisation that had caused the
loss.
9.9       The Convenor observed that in the interest of the industry and country, both the secretaries should spend a lot of
time to resolve the issue. He opined that as a One Time Settlement, substantial amount of LDs should be waived upto
March 31, 2001 taking a cue from Government decision that have been done in the case of UTI and IDBI. The
Committee's decision was to be taken to Board and they may be conveyed the concern of the Committee in this matter.
The Convenor strongly felt that in case the Committee's recommendation was accepted by the Boards, the Committee
would not call meetings time and again to review the issue and everything would be left to the Secretaries of Heavy
Industry and Petroleum & Natural Gas.
CHAPTER–III
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10.       The Committee noted that both the Secretaries of Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and
Petroleum and Natural Gas would have monthly meetings to sort out the problems of finance and delays and Liquidated
Damages would be brought before the independent bodies of the Boards (consisting of independent and non-official
Directors) and those independent bodies would look at it with an open mind. The Committee also observed during the
course of the meetings with various PSUs that delays were sometimes due to involvement of various parties like the
projects of Gandhar where ONGC, Engineering Project India Ltd., Bharat Pumps and Compressors Ltd. and holding
company BYNL had to sort out the problem arising due to supply and testing of compressors. Delays also occurred due
to change in specifications. The Committee also noted that sometimes delays occurred due to labour problem
particularly in the State of Bihar and insurgency problems in Assam. Delays also took place due to delay in importing
engines from abroad due to difficulty in opening Letter of Credit by the supplier company. The Committee feels the Oil
Boards should go into all these aspects and consider the cases where delays on part of the supplier did not contribute to
additional delay before imposing LDs. The Committee recommends that both the Secretaries should look into the details
in their monthly meetings keeping in view the feelings of the Committee. The Committee also recommends that a
quarterly report may be submitted to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry about the
finance, delays and LDs.
11.       The Committee noted during the deliberation that delay in fabrication, supply and commissioning of equipments
contributed to the overall delay in timely completion of the projects. The Committee observes that now delays should be
avoided at all costs. The Committee recommends that a mechanism should be found out by the Department of Heavy
Industry to monitor the work chart of the supplier company and corrective measure should be taken in case delay
occurred at the incipient stage before the delay has any damaging effect on the ongoing project.
12.       Keeping in view the overall industrial scenario, the Committee supports the viewpoint of DHI made by them at
its meeting held on 13th August, 2002 on capacity building in the country itself as the country is opening up and it
would have a different kind of import regime. Companies would be coming to Petroleum sector and construction sector,
and therefore, user sector and capital goods sector should help each other in building a certain capacity to reap benefit of
the new situation.
13.       The Committee strongly feels that in the national interest, a One Time Settlement should be worked out and
substantial amount of LDs may be waived upto 31 March, 2001 to improve the ways and means of Indian companies
taking a cue from the Government decision that has been taken in the case of UTI and IDBI. The Committee strongly
recommends that its concern may be conveyed to the Oil Boards and they may be impressed upon to have a
sympathetic look at the matter. The Committee further observes that in case problems relating to LDs upto 31st
March, 2001 are settled amicably, the Committee would not dilate the matter further and leave it to the
Secretaries of both the Ministries.

Para 4.2 
Recommendation 
        Government should explore ways and means to solve the problem faced by the white fibre manufacturers in the 
absence of proper retting facilities. 
Action Taken Note 
        As a result of the pressure on  retting sites as well as the arduous nature  and drudgery involved , traditional retting
of coconut husk has been on the decline. Instead of retting the whole husk, for considerably long period prior to
defibering, technology has been developed by the Coir Boar d to ret the mechanically extr acted fibre for improving its
quality. This pollution free retting pro cess of green husk fibre using "Coirret", a bacterial consortia, developed by the
Central Coir Research Institute of the Co ir Board, reduces retting period of coir fibre to 3 days. Retting of green hus k
fibre using Coirret has been successfully demonstrated in the white fibre sector. A large quantity of coir fibre and
coconut husk has been retted using Coirret and the popularisation of Coirret retting are being extended to other areas
also. The industry is being encouraged to set up such common facility centres for retting fibre using Coirret.

Para 5.2 
Recommendation 
        The Committee desires that appropriate action may be taken to give a fillip to the mu ch neglected coir industry
and realise its export potential. The Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should take up publicity campaign of coi r
products and launch awareness programmes in these areas for making them popularise and household name.  
Action Taken Note 
        The export of coir products have been registering a su stained growth in the recent past. Several programmes like 
participation in fairs, exhibitions, catalogue shows, ma rket development missions, ex ternal market development
assistance for exporters, new brochures, updated web site , Coir Trade Information Centre, etc. are being implemented
to promote the export of coir products. Necessary outlays ha ve also been included in the Tenth plan for popularising
coir products both in the domestic and export markets.

changed circumstances. This sector can develop through flow of information especially marketing and technology
which is possible through I.T assisted programmes.

coir through collaborative research with reputed institutions like IIT, Bombay, IIT, New Delhi, ATO-DLO, Netharland,

products, R&D activities, etc.

hours a day for the time being, and 24 hours service in due course.

INTRODUCTION
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-ninth Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 84
th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on implementation of Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala.
2.       The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report
at its meeting held on the 17th December, 2002.
NEW DELHI;
17 December, 2002
Dr. P.C.  ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry
 
            
REPORT
The One Hundred-ninth Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 84 th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on implementation of Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala
pertaining to the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha 19
th December, 2002.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the
Report. They have been categorized as follows:
                  (i)    Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:-
Paras : 3.24, 3.27, 3.28, 3.30, 3.32, 3.35, 3.36, 3.41, 4.2, 4.3, 5.5, 5.6, 5.9, 5.11, 6.9, 6.10, 6.12, 6.13,
6.14, 6.15 (Chapter-I).
                 (ii)    Recommendation/Observation which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government's replies : - Para : 1.2, 3.2, 3.37, 6.1, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5  (Chapter-II).

                 (iii)    Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the
Government:- Para : 3.9, 3.10, 3.12, 3.15, 6.6, 6.7, 7.5  (Chapter-III).
                (iv)    Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been
received:- Para : 3.13, 3.20, 3.21, 3.22, 3.42, 6.16, 6.17  (Chapter-IV).
                 (v)    Observations/Recommendations at a Glance.  (Chapter-V).
3. The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries has accepted its recommendation
as mentioned in chapter - I of the Report.
4. In respect of the recommendations made in Chapter-II the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation
advocated by the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries and therefore does not want to pursue further. The Committee
also noted the upward change and modifications in the progress report of Prime Minister Rojgar Yojana and the
schemes respectively.
5. The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations of recommendations contained in Chapter-III and
therefore the Committee desires that the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries would furnish logical explanation in
respect of these recommendations.
6. In respect of recommendation placed in chpater-IV, the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries has either furnished the
interim replies which leaves the Committee yearning for more; the Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry of
Agro & Rural Industries would furnish Action Taken Note in respects of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in
detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
7. The details of the ATR is being discussed in various chapters in the succeeding pages.

be given enhanced targets, and more and more people can be brought under the ambit of the scheme each year.

th Five Year Plan against the plan target of 2.20 lakhs, the year-wise total target

2.3 The Committee observes that there is a great difference between applications recommended and cases sanctioned in
Andhra Pradesh. The downtrend in the number of sanctions is alarming, and the gap between the number of applications
and disbursals has been increasing in Andhra Pradesh. As against the national  average, achievement of the target under

Action  Taken  Rerport
Modified guidelines of the PMRY Scheme under implementation since 1.4.99 do not provide for any minimum
stipulation for projects under industry sector. Despite the enhancement in the projects cost from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 2 lakh
in the revised guidelines, the average loaning under the Scheme continues to be around Rs. 60,000/- per beneficiary,
rendering it difficult to set up any industrial activity out of this. In addition the setting up of projects under industry
sector requires getting power connections, license and NOCs etc. Hence, few people are going into for projects under
industry sector. The self-employment  can mean self employed ventures business and service sectors also. Average
employment generation per unit set up under the PMRY is 1.5% which can either be from industry, service or business
sectors. During the Review Meetings of the PMRY it was deliberated that one of the reasons for rejection of
application/non disbursal of loan was the tendency to adhere the minimum loaning from the industry sector. Since the
aim of the Scheme is to provide self employment, it has been decided by the Government to withdraw the 50% ceiling
on projects from the indsutry sector.

The Committee notes the reply given by the Ministry of A & R I. The Committee, however, is still of the opinion
that in the absence of industry, no asset is created. Since PMRY has been brought under the Ministry of A & R I, it
would be appropriate to give a thought as to how to promote Agro and Rural industries under the scheme.

Action Taken Rerport
The Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana was launched on 2 nd Oct. 93. During 1993-94, the scheme was in operation
only in urban areas of the country. Subsequently, the scheme is being implemented in both urban as well as rural areas
of the country. The guidelines of the scheme do not prescribe that PMRY is basically a Rural programme only.
Similarly, the guidelines of the scheme envisage 22.5 per cent reservation for SC/STs. It is also stipulated in the
guidelines that in case sufficient SC/ST candidates are not available, the State Governments are competent to consider
the applications from other categories.
Article 40 (Chapter VI) of the persons with the disabilities (equal opportunities and fully participation) Act 1995
provide for not less than 3% reservation for disabled in all poverty alleviation programmes. Since PMRY is an
emloyment generation programme and not a poverty alleviation programme, the provision of 3 per cent reservation for
physically disabled persons does not apply to PMRY Scheme.
Further Recommendations
While noting the reply of the Ministry of A&RI, the Committee is disturbed to know that sufficient number of
applications are not coming from the SC/ST candidates. The Committee recommends that awareness programmes about
the PMRY should be regularly held amongst SC/ST candidates. The Committee also recommends that reservations for
disabled perons in the matter of granting loans under PMRY should be included.

contained in the 86
TH Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry Report on
Performance review of Metal  Scrap Trade Corporation Limited (MSTC).

contained in the Report.   These have been categorized as follows:

Recommendations:- 3.1.6 ,  3.1.7, 3.2.5, 3.2.6, 3.2.7, 4.7, 5.4, 6.3, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, 12.6,  and 12.7
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies :

mentioned in Chapter –I of the  Report.

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
           
Recommendations ( Para 3.1.6 and 3.1.7)  
 
MAIN ACTIVITIES
 
3.1.6    The Committee understands the compelling circumstances under which the  MSTC changed its focus of
activities from acting as a selling agent of SAIL to that of maximizing direct marketing (DM) when MSTC got de-
linked from SAIL in 1993.   The Committee appreciates the change in strategy in post-decanalised phase of imports.  
The Committee is pleased to observe the performance of MSTC in direct marketing and hopes that an all out efforts
would be taken by MSTC management to strengthen the marketing activities to improve upon financial performance to
a new commanding heights.
 
3.1.7    The Committee understands the problems being faced by MSTC in carrying out business in a situation when
demand for melting scrap is going down due to increased production of HBI and also because of setting up of scrap
disposal unit-set up by PSUs and other Government departments, MSTC management has to chalk out ‘new strategy’ to
combat the situation.  The Committee feels that provided the Ministry of Steel adhere to the principle of generating an
atmosphere of inter-PSU cooperation and take concrete steps towards assisting MSTC in procuring work-order from
Government PSU, the problems of MSTC could be sorted out to a great extent.  The Committee may be apprised about
the action taken by the Ministry in this direction.
 
Action Taken
 
The observations of the committee have been noted. Marketing activities of the Company have been further
strengthened. In 2001-02, International Marketing Division had achieved sales of Rs.413 crore as against Rs.274 crore
achieved in 2000-01. In 2002-03, in the first six months itself the volume of sales has crossed Rs.600 crore mark.
Financial results have also improved accordingly.
In order to further strengthen the marketing activities, MSTC has installed an e-auction portal and the company
has already registered about 400 customers.  To assist MSTC in procuring work-order from the PSUs, Ministry has also
addressed all PSUs under Ministry of Steel to use the services of MSTC vide letter No.9(13)/2002-MF dated 22.11.02.
KIOCL (Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited) has reported using e.auction of MSTC in case of two lots, in its letter
vide No.D.O.No.D(C)/2002  dated 3.12.02 to Ministry of Steel

Recommendations ( Para 3.2.5, 3.2.6,  and 3.2.7 )  
 
INTERNATIONAL MARKETING
 
3.2.5    The Committee is pleased to note the performance of MSTC in international marketing and appreciates the
strategy of MSTC management for enlarging its import basket in post decanalised phase to compete with other private
parties engaged in similar business.
 
3.2.6    The Committee feels that with the revival of steel industry and undergoing process of strengthening of anti-
dumping the prospect of MSTC in international market would lead to opening of new avenues.
 
3.2.7    The Committee further hopes that MSTC management would chalk out strategy to ensure its survival while
working in adverse condition caused because of lower demand for scrap due to change in charge-mix-owingto increased
availability of DRI and sponge iron.   MSTC has also to learn how to respond and work in a competitive environment.
 
Action Taken
 
The observations/feelings of the committee have been noted.   MSTC is already working successfully in a
competitive environment. In 2001-02, International Marketing Division had achieved sales of Rs. 413 crore as against
Rs. 274 crore achieved in 2000-01. In 2002-03, the volume of sales has crossed Rs.600 crore in the first six months.
Financial results have also improved accordingly.
 
Recommendations  ( Para 4.7)
 
MODERNISATION, RESTRUCTURING AND EXPANSION PROGRAMMES OF MSTC.
 
The Committee notes the steps taken by MSTC management in the field of modernization, restructuring and
expansion programmes of MSTC.  The Committee is of the view that although MSTC is not engaged in the process of
production and is a trading company, however, steps taken towards modernization and restructuring would help in
improving its operational efficiency and managerial effectiveness.  The Committee is of the firm view that
modernization in the process and system of working of the company would have a definite bearing on the physical and
financial performance of the company.  The steps taken to modernize and restructure the communication and expansion
in the domestic as well as international marketing Division would yield positive fruits in the functioning of the
company, the Committee feels so.   The Committee further feels that the efforts made on the part of MSTC management
for enlarging import basket would add to the profitability of the company.
 
Action Taken
 
            The views expressed by the Committee have been noted. 
            With a view to modernize and restructure its operations the company has started an e-auction portal which has
started hosting its tenders on the web-site and E-mail facility has been installed in all branches and regions.   These
measures have already resulted in an improvement in physical and financial performance.
            Some measure of restructuring has been done by merging the purchase & sales transactions both in the domestic
and international trade areas under a common marketing group.  
            The company has also confirmed that measures to enhance the export basket have led to greater profitability.
 
Recommendations ( Para 5.4) 
 
PERFORMANCE OF MSTC
           
            The Committee observes that the activities of MSTC has undergone noticeable change with the changing
scenario of steel industry, change in the Government policy i.e. perspective.   The MSTC which acted earlier as a selling

agency for SAIL in respect of their melting scrap arising, has started to carry the business with the other Government
PSU, SAIL started selling melting scrap directly.    MSTC went, rightly, for strengthening of Direct-marketing when the
Government policy stood for de- canalisation of import.  Although the performance of MSTC suffered to some extent
during this phase of tumultuous change, however, it is the managerial skill, which led MSTC for changing business
gear, and it is the concerted employees commitment which has got a bearing on the physical and financial performance
of the company.   The Committee acclaims the performance of MSTC and hopes that an all out effort on the part of the
management and employees would continue to improve the financial performance of the company to a new zenith.    
                                                                          
 
 
Action Taken
 
            Management as well as employees of MSTC are trying to put in their best to further improve the financial
performance of the company.
Recommendations ( Para 6.3)  
 
 MOU RATING OF THE COMPANY
 
6.3       The Committee observes that MSTC is coming out of the woods and doing excellent performance as is reflected
from MOU rating as awarded by Department of Public Enterprises after taking into various parameters of performance
into consideration.   The Committee wishes its best for MSTC for continuing its excellent performance in forthcoming
years and hopes that MOU system would always act as a catalyst to improve the physical and financial performance of
the company.                                          
 
Action Taken
 
            MSTC is thankful to the Committee for their good wishes and is confident of earning excellent MOU rating in
the years to come.
 
Recommendations ( Para 12.3, 12.4, 12.5,12.6, 12.7) 
 
SWOT ANALYSIS OF MSTC
 
12.3     The Committee observes that MSTC management has given due accordance to the significance of SWOT
analysis in the general working of the company.  The Committee appreciates MSTC management for adhering to the
basic principles and practice of management.   The efforts of re-defining of SWOT analysis on the part of MSTC
management to a praise-worthy step and the Committee hopes that MSTC management would continue to re-orient its
SWOT – analysis as per changing industrial and economic scenario and chalk out its further strategy as per the  outcome
of SWOT analysis.           
                                                           
12.4     The Committee is of the opinion that MSTC management should take advantage of its strength as the company
has minimal fixed overheads expenditure due to optimum manpower with expertise from SAIL equipped with modern
telecommunication and computer.   The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC has good track record for executing
contracts due to its goodwill in the domestic and international market.  Banking upon its company, goodwill/track-
record, MSTC management should make efforts to enhance its market share in domestic as well as international market.
                                                                                                                       
 12.5-   The Committee opines that with the induction of liberalization policy bureaucratic procedures and regulation has
been done away with.  However, MSTC management in tandem with the Ministry of Steel should point out in the ATN
of the present Report the bureaucratic hurdles and Government control having adverse imports on the marketing
capacity of MSTC.   The Committee is of the opinion that MSTC management should have a re-look on the areas of
weakness i.e. induction of latest technological developments, streamlining of the main activities positioning of right
man at the right place in right time, redrafting of corporate goal in the internal market etc.

12.6     The Committee recommends that MSTC management would explore ways and means to capitalize on
opportunities for better financial performance of the Company and it is being hoped that the Ministry of Steel would
extend all possible help to MSTC in this regard.    MSTC management may explore new governess for activities of the
company and consequent changes in the object clearance of the company in order to infect synergy in the overall
working of the company.                                
 
12.7     The Committee further recommends that MSTC management should chalk out strategy for getting rid of threats
being faced by the company.   MSTC management may undertake required steps to inject resilience in the working of
the company in order to combat risk and undertake new works in open and competitive environment.                            
Action Taken
 
Regular updation of the Corporate Plan is indeed necessary and will be taken up in due course by the Company.
The Corporate Plan of the Company was broken down into three phases
                                                Years
            Short-term             -            2001-3
            Mid-term            -            2003-7
            Long-term            -            2007-12
           
It is hoped that most of the goals of the short-term plan will be achieved. While certain goals will be exceeded,
there may be a partial shortfall in goals in certain areas. Revision of the Corporate Plan will be taken up towards the end
of the financial year ending 31.3.2003.
MSTC is making continuous efforts to enhance its market share in the domestic as well as international market,
which is substantiated by the growth in the physical performance of the company for the last five years.
There are no specific bureaucratic hurdles impeding the work of MSTC. In any case, its operations are governed
by commercial considerations approved by the Board of Directors. In fact the status of the Company as a Public Sector
Undertaking enhances its credibility and performance capability because credibility is crucial for a trading house.
Furthermore the support from the Ministry gives the Company an added boost in its domestic marketing operations
particularly with other PSUs and Government Organisations.
            Advice given by the Committee for exploring latest technology for improved performance and also for chalking
out a strategy for getting rid of threats being faced by the Company would be given due attention.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
 
Recommendation (Para 2.3)
 
CAPITAL STRUCTURE
 
2.3       The Committee notes that the company has an authorized Capital of Rs. 5 crore and paid up capital of Rs.2.20
crore as on 31.3.2001 of which approximately 90 per cent of the shares are held by the President of India and the
balance 10 per cent by the members of Steel Furnace Association of India and Iron & Steel Scrap Association of India
and others.  The Committee recommends that MSTC management would take every step to ensure that capital
restructuring of MSTC take place in such a way that return on investment (ROI) is maximum.
 
Action Taken

Under the circumstances, there is no immediate plan of capital restructuring. However, as and when this is done, due

MSTC AS A HOLDING COMPANY.
 
3.3.2    The Committee notes the activities and responsibility of MSTC as a holding company.
 
Action Taken
 
            No recommendation has been made.

ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL
 
Recommendations ( Para 7.4 and  7.5)  
 
Projects/Schemes/Diversification Plans and Financial Requirements.
 
7.4       The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC management is giving due consideration to diversification plans
and entering into joint ventures.   The Committee is of the opinion that in the prevailing market Competitive era,
diversification of activities and projection of business through partnership/joint ventures has almost become a corporate
culture.   MSTC is moving in the right direction by adopting the canons of modern days business practice.   The
Committee hopes that MSTC, whether in existing structure i.e.as a PSU or in the post divested phase would continue its
efforts towards adopting the prevailing precepts and strategy in accordance with changing market scenario.
                                                                                                             
7.5       The Committee notes that financial provisions for completion of plans/schemes of MSTC and at the same time
hopes that all the plans and schemes would be completed without time and cost overrun.           
                                                           
Action Taken
 
Of the Rs.30 crore planned to be spent during 10
th 5-year plan, Rs.14.85 crore have already been invested in
FSNL which is included in BE for 2002-03.  As a technical investment, the Company has also acquired debentures
worth Rs.15.80 crore in Tirumala Rerolling Mills Pvt. Ltd. 
 
While it is MSTC’s hope to emerge as an international trading house, the size of the company (only 280 people),
the low capital base of the company (Rs.2.20 crore – paid up capital) etc. naturally impose a limit.   In trading, ability to
take financial risk and bulking of purchases are important factors.   It is envisaged that the company will continue to
grow but slowly and shall have to depend more on developing its infrastructure for growth.

            The Committee is pleased to note that  MSTC  has  already  invested in Ferro Scrap Nigam Ltd. (FSNL)  to the
tune of Rs.14.85 crore earmarked in BE for 2002-03 out of  the  fund of Rs. 30.00 crore plan to be spent during  Tenth
Five  Year  Plan.  The Committee further notes that the Company has also acquired debentures worth Rs.15.80 crore in
Tirumala   Re-rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd.  The Committee observes that MSTC,  slowly but  steadily, is sailing through  the 
prevailing market competition  in the  liberalized and globalised  economy.  However, the Committee is of the view  
that   MSTC management may undertake  concrete steps  to widen  the capital base of company.  It is further  advised

11.2     The Committee notes that there is no surplus manpower in MSTC at the moment and MSTC is managing in its

strategy of redeployment of manpower in order to have optimum utilization of manpower.  The Committee hopes that

REPORT
Alloy Steel Plant
 
 
 Alloy Steel Plant, a pioneer in the production of alloy and special steel in India, is located at Durgapur, District
Burdwan in the state of West Bengal . Alloy Steels Plant was commissioned in mid 1967 with the objective of
producing and developing various grades of alloy and special steels required by the country.  The plant was designed 
and  engineered by M/s  M.N.  Dastur & Co.  and the production know-how was obtained from M/s Atlas Steel,
Canada.  The integrated production in ASP   commenced from December, 1968 .  The  ingot  steel capacity of the plant
was further augmented by 60.00 tonnes per year by installation of  50 tonnes  arc  furnace with conditioning facilities
and by utilising the second shift of the blooming and  billet mill.  The expansion was completed in March, 1988.  The
capacity of the  plant  has since been expanded from  1,60,000 tpa to 2,60,000  tpa of liquid steel and 1,83,000 tonnes of
saleable steel.    Since its inception, Alloy Steels Plant has not only met the demands of its customers, it has also been
successful in developing many special categories of products required by strategic sectors.  However, despite a much
superior quality edge over its competitors, ASP is facing stiff competition  in the market for selling its products  due to
high cost of production  and  the plant is running loss  on the continuous basis. 
1.2       During the course  of interaction with the Sub-Committee-I,  in the meeting of the Sub-Committee  held  on 14
th
March, 2002,  the Secretary, Ministry of Steel, expressed his concern over  ASP's   performance :-
" The performance of ASP  continues to be disturbing .  It continuous   to make losses.  It is  generally assessed that  in
the prevailing market situation, with the  kind of   technology  and age of equipment that the ASP  has, it would
continue to be a  loss-making unit.  The  disinvestment of ASP is part of the  business   restructuring process of SAIL. 
The Steel Authority has invited bids for  disinvestment. They have invited expressions of interest, but, as of now, the 
assessment is that  there  are no takers.  It is again indicative of the fact that on SAIL's   commercial judgement, ASP is
a loss-making company.  It is something   that the market seems to affirm, because, as  I  said, there has been no 
response to the  advertisement for expressions of interest."
1.3       The Secretary, the Ministry of Steel, further added :-
" There may be  other units which are  on the margin   and with   a change in technology and market conditions,
perhaps, a particular  loss-making unit may turn  into a  profit -making unit.  But  this assessment, unfortunately, is not
right, as far as ASP is concerned."
1.4       The   Committee believes that the Secretary, Ministry of Steel has reasons to express concern over the
operational status of Alloy Steel Plant (ASP).  ASP is facing all odds.  The plant has suffered huge accumulated loss, is
incapable of utilising installed capacity and facilities available, scale of production is unviable, financial performance  is
dwindling,  cost of production is uncompetitive   and it has lost its market.  The disinvestment effect failed as
`Expression of  Interest'  (EOI )  has   evoked  no   response.  Government agencies are not coming forward to help the
plant out.  The performance of plant in the past has been gloomy and at presents the plant is at moribund stage.  The
Committee is of the opinion that the plant may reach to the  point of no return unless a comprehensively considered
revival package is undertaken to improve the operational efficiency   of the plant under  guided   supervision for the
ultimate survival and sustenance of the plant.

perform better  on the financial   front.  ASP is incurring losses year after year and there is  no hope left  for
improvement in its performance, as the plant faces  indomitable problems.  The Committee is  of the  further view that
Government should make a final decision in regard to ASP at the earliest   as ASP is proving a burden  on public purse.
 
7.4       The Sub-Committee was apprised that the reasons for deteriorating physical and financial performance of ASP
are due to following reasons:–
(i)
     High fixed cost
(ii)    Lack of investment in cost effective technology
(iii)  Higher operating cost
(iv)  Under utilization of continuous cast route
(v)   Market condition
(vi)  Higher internal capacity in the country – competition from abroad
(vii)Increase in input cost
(viii)
           Stagnant market prices for our products
(ix)  Dependence on external agencies for major inputs
 
7.5       The reasons, as advocatd by the Ministry of Steel for deteriorating physical and financial performance of ASP,
makes the Committee to recall the proverb      that  "misfortune never comes alone ", as the prevailing  conditions  in
ASP are  the major  stumbling block  for better  functioning of the plant.  The Plant, in itself , is in a dilapidated   
condition  and the Committee is  dismayed, not only at the dwindling financial performance of ASP  but also for the 
plant which is gradually  but surely marching   towards sad demise.

10.0
          Major problems faced by ASP and solution:
 
10.1          The sub-committee was informed that ASP is facing following problems:-
 
i                       Alloy Steels Plant is fundamentally un-competitive because of its  location, low quality of assets and
outdated technology.
ii                     Production at ASP is dependent on the uneconomical low power EAF  route and most of its equipment
is old.
iii                    The market demand for alloy and special steels  in India has stagnated at around 1.4-15 mt over the last
five years and the capacity utilization continues to   be  less than 50 percent  .  The market is high 
fragmented among various small players and ASP'S  market share  is  only 6 percent .
iv                   ASP has a business disadvantage  (vis-à-vis its competitors) in its location in the eastern region, while
nearly 60 percent  of the market demand is from southern and western regions.  ASP has a freight cost
disadvantage vis-à-vis a south based supplier.
v
                     ASP has lost volume steadily, as the requirement of inter-plant transfers have come down, on account of
economic considerations.
vi                   High manpower cost and high overheads.
 
10.2     As a result of inherent problems being faced by ASP, the plant has the trend of decreasing sales realization due
to high variable cost of production   compared to the competitors. SAIL is finding it very difficult to fund the losses of
Alloy Steel Plant, since SAIL'S overall financial performance itself is uncomfortable.
 
10.3     The Committee observes that the problems being faced by ASP are deeply- rooted  and pose the real threat for
the survival and sustenance of the   plant   under the prevailing environment.  There are the   reasons to believe that

16.0
          Disinvestment  of ASP
 
16.1            Considering  ASP’s financial performance   in the  past  and no  strong possibility of  improvement,
divestment  of ASP would have helped  SAIL in reducing its financial burden.   Accordingly, with the approval of GOI,
an advertisement inviting  EOI  was issued on 26.6.0 . The last date for receipt    of EOI  was 24
th August, 2001. 
However, the advertisement for inviting  EOI  has  evoked no response from any interested bidders.  Therefore, in view
of the above, it can be concluded   divestment  of ASP is not a feasible proposition. Given the accumulated losses by
ASP and its current performance, the divestment process has not attracted interest from any suitable bidder.  Hence, as
of now, the divestment possibility may be taken as closed.  The matter was  discussed in the last meeting of Committee
of Secretaries  (COS)   has   also noted that the divestment of ASP does not  appear   feasible  in the near  future and has
recommended that  all options  in this regard may be  worked out for consideration of CCEA. In view  of the fact that
the divestment of ASP does not  appear   feasible  in the near  future,  it has now been decided to follow a 2 pronged
strategy   vis.,
 
i
           Special thrust on reducing manpower; and
ii         To reduce level of operations at ASP, based on market conditions/financial aspects
 
16.2.    The Committee understands that, considering ASP's financial performance in the past and no strong possibility
of improvement, in future ASP is proving a nuisance SAIL in general and a burden on government's treasures. 
Therefore, efforts were made for divestment of ASP.  However, market proved much more prudent and Expression of
Interest (EOI) evoked   no response for purchasing the ailing plant of SAIL.  ASP is dwindling further, SAIL is not in a
position to invest on ASP , and Government   is not in a position to inject `new lease of life'  to the plant, which seems to
be at the  moribund stage.
 
16.3.    The Committee welcomes the two pronged strategy i.e. rationalisation of manpower and scaling down
production as per market demand.  The Committee hopes that strategy undertaken would improve operational efficiency
of ASP.

19.0
          Steps required for Revitalization of operational efficiency of ASP
 
19.1     The Committee is of the opinion that Alloy Steels Plant is a  pioneer in the production of stainless steel in India,
and   its products are  being  used by the Defence, Railway, Space Research Organisations, Nuclear Power Plants .
When India was debarred to import alloy steels required for Bofors Cannon Shells during Kargil conflict and high
quality special stainless steel required for  Atomic Research Centres ,after the Nuclear Test at Pokhran, it was ASP,
which  came forward to produce all these materials required at the moment of national crisis. Therefore, the Committee
feels that it would  be a national loss if ASP, a holder of ISO-9002 Certificate , is thrown away.

19.2          Merger of DSP and ASP
 
The Committee views thatthe close proximity of Alloy Steels Plant and Durgapur Steel Plant, under the same
organisations – SAIL, is a matter of great advantage. ASP is utilizing scrap skull, C. O. gas, electricity,  water, dolomite,
oxygen from DSP.  It also utilises Hot Metal/Liquid Steel, Ingot, Blooms & Billets as input materials. The two sister
plants of SAIL are having common township and Hospital, under the control of same Managing Director. Therefore ,
the Committee feels that the possibility of merger of DSP and ASP may be explored . This plant could be made more
cost effective by utilizing the in-house facilities of the two SAIL Plants, ASP & DSP. This requires  more close
supervision and effective co-ordination. This should not be a difficult job since the two plants are under the control of
same Managing Director.  What is needed, is the will of SAIL to run both the Plants, making best use of the technical
arrangements already prevailing to make both the Plants economically viable.
 
19.3     The suggestion of R&D, SAIL, to install an AOD at ASP for improving quality of stainless steel and EMS at
concast shop for production of Defence & Automobile requirements, should be examined The other suggestion of
technical experts like Dastur & Co. to install a Billet Caster, Wire Rod Mill and modernize the Forge Shop , may be
taken into  consideration .
 
19.4     The Sub-Committee was apprised of the fact that after installation of continuous shop in various steel plants, the
availability of mild steel scrap has drastically gone down.  ASP's requirement of scrap from different plants is 10,000
MT per month.  Following is the need from sister plants to sustain production level.
            1. Bokaro Steel Plant :   4500 MT
            2. Durgapur Steel Plant:    5500 MT
19.5     The special steels produced in integrated steel plant is very cost effective.  In ASP, is also exploring the
possibility of getting the inputs from Durgapur Steel Plant in the form of ingots/Basic Oxygen Furnace Liquid
steel/Rolled or Cast Billet & Blooms to the tune of 6000 MT per month.  At present it is at the level of 1500 T per
month. This is being perused at various levels in SAIL and  they  are sure to get this support within SAIL.
 
19.6
          Utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel  
 
The Committee is of the view that  to reduce the cost of production of ASP products, a substantial quantity of
ASP customer’s need can be meted out by utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel made through BOF route as well as
Ingots, Bloom and Billets.  The Committee hopes production of ASP may be carried on  with close co-ordination with
Durgapur Steel Plant.  With transfer of liquid steel from DSP to the tune of yearly 50,000 MT monthly 4500 MT.  To
facilitate the transfer of this Steel, necessary arrangement may  be made.
 
19.7          Installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS
 
The  installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS, which is essential for regaining lost market in the
automobile sectors of the Eastern Region , may be examined.
 
19.8     Use of DSP-ASP route
Electric Arc Steel making is a costly process which should   be sparingly used  at  ASP.  ASP should utilize
ASP's finishing facilities to produce around 90,000 tonnes of steel from DSP-ASP route per annum to make a cost
effective contribution. 
19.9            Nominal   Investment
ASP has a large potential in production of high quality  forgings   upto 12,000  TPA.  A nominal   investment to
augment the Unit in order to bring in high returns can be considered on priority. An  investment  of around Rs.2-3
Crores can enlarge product- mix as per market requirement .
19.10   Closure of Unviable Unit
The operational efficiency of both the production units viz Plate Mill & Bar Mill should be evaluated, and if

Alloy Steels  Plant  is a major supplier of steel products to Defence, Railways and almost all the important
