Professionals, and Academicians. In order to meet the requirements of technical inputs the Task Force has been
reconstituted by inducting professionals/academicians from the reputed institutions.
7.11The following steps have been taken by Department of Public Enterprises to make the MoU system more effective.
        (i)  Instead of confining the scope of MoU system to the traditional approach of arriving at certain figures under the
static parameters, the PSEs are advised to pay adequate attention to the dynamic parameters like
productivity, customer satisfaction, HRD, quality improvement and R&D to be included as prominent
performance indicators.
        (ii)The parameter on project implementation with suitable weight is required to be included in the draft MoUs.
        (iii)     It has also been emphasized to pay more attention on the strategic issues which are very crucial for the
growth of the PSEs over a long period of time and PSEs had been asked to prepare their strategic plans in
consultation with the Administrative Ministries.
        (iv)Efforts have been made to finalize all MoUs before the commencement of the next financial year, so that the
targets are known to the managements of MoU signing PSEs in advance and they are able to develop
coherent strategies to achieve those targets.
        (v)  In order to make the MoU negotiation meetings more meaningful and effective, it is ensured that the
participation from the Administrative Ministries/Departments is at a senior (Additional/Joint Secretary)
level.
7.12Some of the measures of financial and operational autonomy delegated to Boards of MoU signing PSEs are as
follows :
        1.   Capital Expenditure : MoU signing PSEs having Gross Block of over Rs. 200 crores can incur expenditure of
Rs. 50 crores on additions, modifications and new investments and Rs. 100 crores on replacement, renewal
of assets without prior approval of the Government provided they meet certain conditions.
        2.   Wage Revision : MoU signing PSEs can finalize wage revisions within broad guidelines laid down by DPE.
        3.   Incentive Scheme : MoU signing PSEs can evolve incentive schemes within the broad guidelines laid down by
DPE subject to the condition that the total of bonus and incentive shall not exceed to the 35% of the wages.
        4.   Transfer of Functional Directors : MoU signing PSEs have powers to transfer functional directors from one
charge to another in consultation with the Secretary of the Administrative Ministry and with the prior
approval of the Minister.
7.13The Committee observes that the investment decisions to create public sector units were based on social cost
benefit analysis. Moreover most of the public sector enterprises were not expected to maximize profits. However,
the social cause no longer being a vogue, and market forces replacing the old economy with the ushering in of
liberalization, the performance of PSEs has to be evaluated on their economic performance. The Public Sector
Enterprises's performance, therefore, should be evaluated based on their financial profit.
7.14MoU should have relation to financial well being of a PSEs. Financial parameters are must to evaluate the
state of health of a PSE. However, the Committee observes that PSEs which are even under performing are
graded as good, very good or excellent depending upon the level of their achievements under the MoU target.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that financial performance of PSEs should be the main criteria for
rating their achievement.
7.15The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad hoc Task Force on the basis
of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the target by the predetermined
stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as 'excellent' and when the target is just met, the enterprise is ranked as 'very
good'. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either 'good' or 'fair' or 'poor'. Ranking
depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
7.16The Committee appreciates the efforts of DPE to make the MoU system more effective. Still much more has
to be done in this direction. It is more important that dynamic parameters like productivity, customer
satisfaction, HRD, quality improvement and R&D are taken into account. Department of Public Enterprises

should constantly endeavour to make MoU system as an instrument of improvement.
NON-OFFICIAL DIRECTORS IN BOARDS OF PSEs
8.     Part-time non-official Directors are individuals of repute having experience in different fields. On their
appointment as Directors the Boards of these PSEs get the benefit of their guidance and advice in the management of
the Company. Their appointment has helped in introducing transparent and effective systems of internal monitoring
through Audit Committees. The performance of PSEs depends upon a number of other critical factors such as its
competitive strength, organisational structure, the changes in its business environment, etc. Thus, it would be very
difficult to correctly quantify the improvement in performance of PSEs due to the delegation of powers mentioned
above. But enhanced autonomy to the PSEs certainly helps the managements to take quick decisions which are very
essential to meet the challenges of business especially under the emerging competitive economic environment.
8.1   Instructions have been issued by the Department of Public Enterprises to induct non-official part-time Directors on
the Boards of PSEs. The non-official Directors are drawn from public men, technocrats, management experts and
consultants, and professional managers in industry and trade with high degree of proven ability. The number of such
Directors should be at one-third of the actual strength of the Board. In the cases of listed Companies headed by
Executive Chairman, the number of non-official (Independent) Directors should be half of the Board.
8.2   The Navratna and Miniratna PSEs can exercise the enhanced powers only after their Boards and professionalised
by inducting adequate number of non-official Directors. A Search Committee consisting of Chairman Public Enterprises
Selection Board (PSEB), Secretary (DPE), Secretary of the Administrative Ministry concerned and eminent persons
from outside has been set up for selection of non-official Directors for the Navratna and Miniratna PSEs. The Search
Committee has been meeting frequently to make selections of non-official Directors.
8.3   Enhanced operational and financial powers are delegated to Navratna PSEs and Miniratnas. The enhanced power
enables these PSEs to take decisions in investment and operational matters without having to seek the approval of the
Government apart from cutting down delay in decision making, the efficiency as well as accountability of the Boards of
Directors have increased due to delegations of these powers. The enhanced powers are not available to sick PSEs.
8.4   The Committee observes that non-official part-time directors are drawn from various segments of society
i.e. public men, technocrats, management experts etc. However, they discharge their duties for no monetary gain.
Committee has the apprehension that this may play down on their accountability to the Board of PSE of which
they are members. DPE should look into this aspect.
PURCHASE  PREFERENCE  POLICY
9.     The Purchase reference Policy has been extended upto 31.3.2004. The Committee had earlier recommended that
Department of Public Enterprises should apprise the Committee about non-implementation of the policy, if any, by any
PSE. But Department of Public Enterprises have not so far complied with the recommendation. The Committee
understands that certain PSEs are not adhering to the Policy. Violation of the Policy by PSEs makes mockery of the
Policy which have been notified with the cabinet approval.
9.1   The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should apprise the Committee about the
non-implementation of the Policy for the last one year.
VOLUNTARY  RETIREMENT  SCHEME
10.   In the present system, funds are allocated to the central PSEs at 17.5% rate of interest per annum in case of
working capital loans including funds for VRS and at 13.5% rate of interest for other loans. In the falling interest rate
regime, transfer of such high cost funds severely impacts the balance sheet position of each PSE precipitating financial
crises. The Committee feels such high rate of interest attached to VRS funds have an adverse effect on the balance sheet
of the companies and it should be corrected.
10.1The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should revert to the old system of permitting VRS funds
as grants. It would be a much needed relief as loss making and marginally profit making companies are in urgent
need of shedding their oversized manpower.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
        The Committee finds that there has been constant increase in the plan allocation of CRR scheme over the earlier
years. As against Rs. 6.75 crores allocated in RE 2001-02, an allocation of Rs. 8.50 crores was made in BE 2002-03 for
CRR which was taken up by DPE since 1st April, 2001. Earlier it was dealt by the Department of Industrial Policy and
Promotion. In BE 2003-04, the amount has been increased to Rs. 9.00 crores. This is the third year since the scheme
commenced. The Committee recommends that in view of the increasing trends in the plan allocation for CRR scheme
and time factor, a suitable mechanism for appraisal of the scheme should be evolved by DPE so as to evaluate the
results in this regard and assess the desired impact of the scheme.(Para 3.4)
        The Committee observes that North Eastern Area and Sikkim comprising of seven States i.e. Arunachal Pradesh,
Meghalaya, Nagaland, Assam, Tripura, Manipur and Mizoram, is an economically and industrially backward area. The
allocation of Rs. 1.00 crore for the area for CRR scheme is not enough considering the vast area to be covered under the
scheme. If the area has to be developed, entrepreneurship has to be given a fillip. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the plan allocation for North Eastern area should be further increased so as to open more training
centres in these areas to impart training to the persons and have a wider coverage of the scheme.

        The Committee observes that the issue has been under consideration of the Ministry for the last one year and a

REPORT
 
 
1.         The Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises) is responsible for promoting
engineering industry in the country and development and growth of capital goods.  The industries covered by this Department
provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the
requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping,
paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of  wide range of intermediate engineering
products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes.  There are 49  Public  Sector Enterprises (PSEs)
under the administrative charge of the Department.
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of engineering/capital goods,
consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department
of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8234.00 crores till 31st March, 2002,  employing about 1.18  lakh persons.
1.2       The Department holds interactions with various Industry Associations and evolves plans for the growth of the industry.
The Department also assists industry through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and trade, technological
collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

2.4      The Committee finds that though the projections of the PSEs were  higher, only limited support was provided by the

guarantee etc. The Committee also impresses upon  the Government  to fully  utilize the funds provided and avoid  the previous
years  experience in this regard.

B.E. 2003-04. An allocation of Rs.25.00 crores under non-plan budget has also been made in B.E. 2003-04 for the purpose.
3.1       The allocated funds are to be utilized for funding significant projects on automotive safety and emission testing, on
creating infrastructure and validating performance of the components and  vehicles in terms of global emission, safety, tolerance
norms being prescribed by Economic Commission for Europe etc. Introduction of higher safety and emission norms is not
possible in the country without commensurate testing facilities being available. It is in this context that this allocation becomes
really meaningful and important.
3.2       Following delicensing of automotive industry in 1993, this sector has made great advances and has opened up to FDI.
The investment  in the industry is Rs.50,000 crores up to the end of March, 2000. The research activities in the automotive
sector have also comparatively intensified. All auto companies are having their own R&D laboratories to meet their limited
requirements. The infrastructure at Automotive Research Association of India, Pune, (ARAI), has also been considerably
upgraded to meet common requirements of all auto manufacturers. However, the total expenditure by auto industry at present on
its R&D activities is paltry 0.2 per cent. Considering the quality of automobiles in India as compared with the automobiles
manufactured in advanced countries, this expenditure on R&D is rather meager and needs to be increased considerably so that
the automobiles manufactured in India are of the same standard and quality as in developed countries. The improved quality of
automobiles will not only benefit the domestic consumers but will also enable the industry to export in larger numbers and
compete effectively.
3.3       The Government also has to provide financial assistance in this sector. The Committee notes that R&D has not received
the same importance it deserves in so far as allocation of funds is concerned. Although, tax holiday has been extended to R&D
companies up to March 31, 2004, but this measure is perhaps not adequate. What is required is enhanced allocation of funds 
collected as the cess on auto vehicles in order to intensify testing and research activities in the auto sector. The allocation to the
Ministry for R&D falls short of the projected demand i.e. Rs.1500 crores in the coming five to seven years. The Ministry was
allocated Rs.70 crores only during 2002-03. This amount has been reduced to Rs.50 crores for the year 2003-04 (rs.25 crores as
plan and Rs.25 crores as non-plan).
3.4       The Committee observes that with the introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards,
upgradation of automotive testing facilities is critically needed for further growth of automotive industry in the country. There is
also a need to look at other areas of product and process related research with a view to propelling India’s automotive industry
into a higher league and for surviving the import surge under WTO regime.  The required level of R&D  can be achieved only
by enhanced funding.  It is a fact that the Government is collecting automotive cess at the rate of 0.125%  per cent over and
above excise duty on vehicles. But since inception in 1984-85,  allocation of funds has been meager and much less than the
actual collection. Now  a comprehensive project on upgrading the testing infrastructure in the country is proposed to be
implemented at a cost of Rs.1500 crore. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the Government should enhance allocation
under cess to the extent of full amount collected. The Government should also allocate in two installments the entire unallocated

BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICAL LTD.
14.       Bharat Heavy Electricals ltd. (BHEL) was set up primarily to meet the needs of the power sector in the country. At

120th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/120threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:06]
present, BHEL has 14 manufacturing divisions, 9 service centres and 4 Power sector regional centres in addition to a large
number of project sites spread all over India and abroad, enabling BHEL to serve the customers and the country promptly and
effectively. Besides. BHEL has a Corporate R&D complex at Hyderabad, HRD Institute at Delhi and Research Centre in all
manufacturing plants. .
14.1     BHEL manufactures over 180 products under 30 major product groups and meets the need of core sectors like power,
industry, transmission, transportation, defence, telecommunications, oil business, etc.Power is the core sector of B HEL and
comprises of thermal, nuclear, gas, diesel and  hydro business. BHEL built sets account for nearly 65% of the country's total
installed power generating capacity.
14.2     BHEL has made a major contribution in the areas of process industry, transportation, transmission, telecommunication,
non-conventional energy and other new products.  BHEL contributes major capital equipment and systems like captive power
plants, centrifugal compressors, drive turbines, pumps, heat exchangers, electric motors, valves, heavy castings and forgings,
etc. to the core industries viz. cement, metallurgical, mining, refineries, petro-chemicals, chemicals, etc. The Company has also
emerged as a major supplier of controls and instrumentation systems. In the transmission sector, besides producing high voltage
transformers and switchgear,  BHEL supplies equipment for high voltage direct current systems. The Company has also been
supplying oil-field equipment to ONGC and Oil India. Most of the trains in Indian Railways are equipped with BHEL's traction
control equipment. BHEL also manufactures AC/DC locos, battery powered road vehicles, OHE cars and motorized.
14.3     The Committee observes that power manufacture sector accounts for major business of BHEL(70%) apart from Industry
(20% ) and international market (10%) .  There is a great potential in power sector due to gap  between demand  and supply of
power.  But due to low investment , projects are not  coming up fast .  State electricity Board are major handicap in this regard.
14.4     The Committee therefore, recommends that  with the target of achieving 10,000 MW of additional capacity in power
generation by 2010 , there  is a need  to make huge  investments in the power sector .  Government of  India should  ensure that 
all possible steps  are taken  to see that  this sector does  not suffer due to resource  crunch Department of Heavy industry should
consider the matter regarding liquidation of outstanding dues of BHEL to be paid by SEBs afresh.  Committee hopes that  
Electricity   Bill will    be cleared by Parliament soon which will  improve the working of  SEBs and streamline their operations
which will be of help to BHEL also.  As regards the import of technology and operation of multinational companies
participating in bidding for large contracts in infrastructure building, suitable measures/precautions are needed to safeguard  the
Indian companies like BHEL and also reduce outflow  of capital from the country.  
14.5     Citing the example of China the Committee was apprised that whenever a technology is  brought in,  Chinese Govt.
stipulate that  over-seas company must associate a Chinese company in the process of manufacturing.  When a large  contract is

120th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/120threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:06]
awarded to over-seas non-Chinese company, China makes it a requirement that a part of that business  i.e.40  per cent must
come to  Chinese company.  Similarly, Malaysia has got ‘Bhumiputra policy’.   Bhumiputra Company,  which is registered in
Malaysia, will  have to be associated.  When technology is imported, local company must be associated.  China is doing it very
efficiently,   whereas,  India is  not doing it.  The technologies are brought in and  a local company is associated with the
technology and, gradually, indigenisation happens.
14.6     The Committee ,therefore recommends that when technologies are outsourced, Indian Government should make it
mandatory that  an Indian company is associated with the foreign partner in order to   absorb the technology  to the local needs.
The foreign firm  should have a tie-up with an Indian company. Multinational corporations are often bidding for large contracts
of infrastructure building etc. in the country. The Government should consider imposing conditions requiring involvement of at
least one Indian business entity.
14.7     The Committee was also apprised  that in order to create  capacity  for power generation BHEL must get order within
one-and-half years ahead  of the schedule.  If orders  are not placed  to BHEL beforehand, it will not be able to manufacture

 1.9 Cost components of products produced by NMDC
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC management has introduced the muli-skilling concept to reduced the
fixed cost. The Committee also notes that various managerial controls measures are at work to reduce the cost of production.
The Committee desires that the Ministry of Steel, in its action Taken Note of the present Report, would furnish the detail as
to what extent the cost reduction measure entailed tangible result.
(PARA 10.4)
 Action Taken
 
The cost reduction measure undertaken by company is given below:
 
(a)
    fixing of standard cost at the beginning of the year for internal target production
(b)   comparison of actual cost with the standard cost monthly at project level
(c)    remedial measures to contain the cost at project level.
(d)   Monthly review of cost at Head Office by the management
 
Standard Cost per unit of iron ore / diamonds is prepared at the beginning of the year on the basis of production and
dispatch / sales targets finalized in the Corporate Plan meeting.  Project wise standard cost is projected considering the bench
marks in respect of each element of expenditure.  The bench marking is done considering the best of the physical parameters
achieved in the previous year, the average of previous five years or the standard set for the previous year, whichever reflects

efficiency, economy and effectiveness.  These physical parameters are regularly monitored by concerned departments viz
Production, Industrial Engineering and Finance  at the project as well as at Head Office.  The physical norms thus
established, for consumption such as ‘powder factor’ for explosives, ‘consumption per tonne of excavation’ for drill bits,
tyres & tubes, stores/spares , power etc., and the latest landed cost of the materials at the time of preparation of standard cost
are taken into account to project the expenditure for the target production quantity.  
 
The standard cost as estimated above are reviewed at HO by Directors and approved by the Chairman for
communicating the same to the units for monitoring the actual cost periodically.
 
There after, the actual cost of production is compared with the standard cost periodically at the project level.  The said
procedure of fixing standard costs is being followed consistently and wherever required, the same is being suitably modified
so that effective cost control can be made by the Corporation.
 
At the projects, during monthly review meetings of all HOD’s, the cost of production is discussed for minimizing the 
costs keeping in view the standard cost envisaged for that year.   At Head Office also, every month, the actual cost up to the
month is reviewed with previous year cost as well as standard cost and deviations are brought to the notice of the
management.   The actual cost of production vis-à-vis the standard cost, is also discussed and reviewed in the Annual / Mid-
Term Corporate Meetings.
 
            In addition, the units prepare cost sheets periodically covering all the cost centers and circulate to the respective
departments.   The same is reviewed in the project review meetings for taking remedial action wherever necessary.

3.3 Major customers of NMDC in domestic and foreign market and need of autonomy for NMDC in export promotion i.e.
direct export by NMDC
 
            The Committee notes that NMDC sells 55% of its production for the domestic market while 45% is being sold out to
international market. The Committee wonders that even in the age of liberalization and globalization the Government
continues with policy of allowing the service of canalizing agency. De-canalization should have followed theliberalization
policy. While de-canalisation applies with one of PSUs under the Ministry of steel i.e. Metal Scrap Trade Corporation
Limited (MSTC) and the same principle has not been applied in the case of NMDC. As per the existing system, Iron-Ore is
to be exported through canalizing agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to Iron ore with 65% Fe content and above
whereas NMDC has got more quantity of Iron Ore lying in its pit head with less than fifty  five percent Iron content for
which international market is available but the same is not explored by NMDC. Therefore, the Committee feels that, it
would be in the fitness of things that NMDC is given complete autonomy in the best-interest of the Company. The
Committee feels NMDC be allowed to direct export to the countries other than the purchaser from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pak
and South Korea, NMDC has already exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 Lakh tones in 1999-2000, 9.65 Lakh tones
in 2000-01, and thus experience so gained, would proved handy to NMDC in direct export of Iron-ore. 
(PARA 21.11.4)
 
    Government is aware of the need for de-canalization of iron-ore. However, in view of the Long Term Agreement for
export of iron ore by MMTC, Govt. has decided that the existing arrangement for export of high quality iron –ore (with Fe
content of 645 and above) through MMTC may continue.
 
            After government intervention, an agreement was reached as per which NMDC has been entrusted with more
responsibility for all operational matters, including rail handling up-to loading into the ship. MMTC also agreed to reduce
the service charge from 5-6% of FOB to 3% on FOB value. This agreement has given NMDC a large role in export
operations.
 
             For the year 2002-03, NMDC has now been permitted to export 30  LMT (15 LMT from Bailadila and 15 LMT
from Donimalai). NMDC has also been granted export license for the following quantities:
 
Year Bailadila Donimalai Total

Further Recommendation
 
The Committee is of the view that NMDC should be allowed to direct export to the countries rather than through
MMTC to the order of substantial quantity.  Time frame for how long export of iron ore through MMTC would continue has
not been indicated.  The Committee feels that functional autonomy given to NMDC in regard to direct export would enhance
the operational efficiency of the company in direct marketing.

Observations /Conclusions/ Recommendations of the Committee at a glance
 
3.1 MOU rating of NMDC
 
The Committee is of the view that the NMDC management should reflect various financial ratios and expression to
stress its claim for being conferred the status of Navratna.  It is expected that the Ministry of Steel would advocate with the
Department of Public Enterprises for giving the status of Navratna to NMDC .  The Committee is of the considered view
that conferring the status of Navratna to NMDC would encourage the management and workers for improving upon the
physical and the financial performance of the company further.
 
3.2 Formation of Council of Mining enterprises
 
             The Committee understands that Mineral Advisory Council has been set up by the Department of Mines chaired by
Union Minister for Mines and it meets once in a year to discuss the problems being faced by Mining Industry.  Intention of
the Committee behind recommending the formation of Council of ONGC, MECL, IBM, GSI, GAIL and NMDC is to
provide a platform for frequent formal and informal discussion on various issues to solve the problems of mining operation
and going beyond the jurisdiction of Department of Mines and covering to the areas of coal, steel, petroleum and mines as
well.  Moreover, the formation of the proposed Council would provide a platform for inter PSUs co-operation and through
mutual discussions the mutual problems could be solved.
While FIMI is an association of various mining associations which gathers data and information regarding mining
operation and interface interact with the government bodies for redeeming  of grievances pertaining to mining operations. 
Therefore, neither the FIMI nor the Mineral Advisory Council is the substitute for the proposed council of ONGC,
MECL, IBM, GSI, GAIL and NMDC.
 
3.3 Major customers of NMDC in domestic and foreign market and need of autonomy for NMDC in export promotion i.e.
direct export by NMDC
 
The Committee is, however, of the view that NMDC should be allowed to direct export to the countries rather than
through   MMTC to the order of substantial quantity. Time frame how long export of iron ore through MMTC would
continue has not been indicated.  The Committee feels that functional autonomy given to NMDC in regard to direct export
would enhance the operational efficiency of the company in direct marketing.
 
3.5 Key concern Areas of Mining Industry in general and problems being faced by NMDC in particular and help required
from the Government.
 
Inflated mileage on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line
 
The Committee welcomes the reduction of inflated freight on k.k. line by 10% i.e. from 30% to 20% it is being
hoped that the Ministry of Steel could make effort for rationalization of railway freight further so that it could further come
down. 
 
3.6 Problems at Chennai Port
 
The Committee feels that the Ministry of Steel should have constant interaction with the management of NMDC and
accordingly resolve their problems at the first instance.  Therefore, it is reiterated that the Ministry of Steel should facilitate

REPORT
         Steel is crucial to the development of any modern economy and is concerned to be the backbone of the human
civilization. Since steel industry is technologically a complex industry having strong forward and backward linkages in
terms of material flow and income generation, all major economies are not invariably characterized by the existence of a
strong steel industry, but also the growth of many of these economies have been largely shaped by the strength of their
steel industry during their early stages of development. Some of the newly industrializing countries like South Korea,
China and Brazil among others have built up substantial capacities not only to support their rapidly growing domestic
economies, but also to export significantly to mark their presence in the international market. India, after independence,
embarked on a massive industrialization programme wherein need was left for self-reliance in steel. Accordingly, large
plants were set up and capacities were created, mostly in the public sector.
1.2    The liberalization of the economy since 1991-1992 has witnessed a spate of new capacity additions in the private
sector because a quantum change took place in the steel industry. Steel Plants in private sector are coming up and
producing two-third of the total finished products. Long-term growth prospect of steel industry is encouraging a large
number of people to set up Greenfield capacities with modern technology in the private sector. These capacities with
state of the art technology involve lower concession costs than the units in the public sector. Under an era of
liberalization and with the lowering of international trade barriers only economic consideration are determining external
trade, both imports as well as exports. Competitiveness of the industry has become crucial not only for increasing exports
but also in competing with imports in the domestic market as tariff barriers are being reduced in a phased manner. As a
matter of fact the steel industry in India has been adversely affected by the rationalization and reduction of duties
resulting in lower tariff protection against imports, South East Asian currency crises, Russian Rouble devaluation, lower
international prices and the consequent meltdown, dumping due to lack of demand. Global Steel Industry for the major
part of 2001 remained a victim of slow down in demand, sliding price levels, low realizations, losses and/or falling
profits. However, from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase, with the gradual firming up of
international prices and demand. These trends largely persist to date. The year 2003 may well see a price rise in the
domestic and the international steel market.
1.3    The Ministry of Steel has to play a crucial role in ensuring harmonious and integrated growth of steel sector. The
main functions of Ministry of Steel are as under:-
         (a)    co-ordination of the growth of the Iron and Steel Industry (including Re-rolling Mills, Alloy Steel and Ferro
Alloy industries, Refractories) both in the Public and Private Sector.
         (b)    formulation of policies in respect of production, pricing, distribution, import and export of iron and steel and
Ferro Alloys;
         (c)    planning, development and control of and assistance to the entire iron and steel industry in the country; and
         (d)    development of input industries relating to iron ore, manganese ore, refractories etc., required mainly by the
steel industry.
1.4    Besides the Secretariat, the Ministry of Steel has an attached office viz. the office of the Development
Commissioner for Iron and Steel (DC I & S) located at Calcutta and its four Regional Offices located in New Delhi,
Calcutta, Chennai and Mumbai. Under the administrative control of Ministry of Steel the following Public Sector
Undertakings are functioning:-
         (i)     Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL).
         (ii)     Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. (KIOCL), Bangalore.
         (iii)    National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. (NMDC), Hyderabad.
         (iv)    Hindustan Steel Works Construction Ltd. (HSCL), Calcutta.

5.0    ECONOMIC PHILOSOPHY BEHIND BUDGET PROPOSALS FOR 2003-04:IMPACT OF
GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALISATION ON THE STEEL INDUSTRY
5.1    Replying to the Committee’s query as regards the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals 
2003-04 and impact of globalisation and liberalisation on Steel Industry the Ministry of Steel explained that the Union
Budget 2003-04 is reform-oriented and its fundamental aim is to create conditions for growth. While globalisation is an
avowed objective of the government policy, the government has also taken note of the possible pitfalls on its way and
has sought to provide, sufficient safeguards to various sectors in the economy especially those considered vulnerable.
The aim of the budget proposals has also been to rationalise certain provisions, bring harmony in fiscal structures related
to various sectors and create a more efficient tax regime.
5.2    The overall objective is visible in the measures for the steel industry. However, given the complexity in the
industry, there are areas where the measures have adversely affected the steel industry. These include raising (with a
view to rationalisation) of import duty rates of raw materials like metallurgical coke and nickel. The reduction of peak
duty rate to 25 per cent from 30 has also reduced the nominal protection rate for the finished steel products in the
country. Further, the elimination of the 5 per cent duty differential as a result of this measure between Hot Rolled Coils
and other downstream products like CR and galvanised sheets, will affect the economics of the stand alone CR and
galvanising mills. Further, although the decision to withdraw the facility given to the integrated steel plants to pay excise
duty on their ex-plant prices, irrespective of where they sell from, is in line with the overall government policy, the
specific conditions in which these plants operate do not appear to have been taken into account, especially the fact that
these plants are close to mines and in backward areas and their markets are located far away.
5.3    The Committee is pleased to note that the Union Budget 2003-04 is reform-oriented and its fundamental aim is to
create conditions for growth. However, it is expected that the Ministry of Steel would seriously and effectively take up
the issue of suitable amendment in the tax structure with the Ministry of Finance so as to rectify some of the tax
rationalisation proposals, which are adversely affecting the steel industry.
5.4    Elaborating the impact of globalisation and liberalisation on the Steel Industry, the Ministry of Steel added that
globalisation is an ongoing process and the steel industry in India has been subject to this steady process of liberalisation
and globalisation since 1991. From 1991, various economic reform measures started changing the contours of regulation
in this important industry. In a series of reforms in 1991, the government removed the steel industry from the list of
industries reserved for the public sector. The sector was opened up further by the removal of the erstwhile licensing
system. Except for certain locational and environmental matters, new capacity development efforts in the country do not
require any clearance of the government.
5.5    The Committee was given an understanding that the Steel industry has also been benefiting from the reforms in the
capital market in tapping investible resources with case and without having to go through various government clearances
that characterised the erstwhile-regulated regime. The simultaneous reforms in the economy, in the form of removal of
the licensing system for imports and exports and reduction in import tariffs and making the country’s currency fully
convertible on trade account brought in a sea change in the overall environment of business. Much of the changes were
brought in to tune the system to the guidelines and requirement of the World Trade Organisation. The industry faced
corresponding liberalisation in their market for raw materials as the domestic and the external frontiers were opened up.
5.6    While the steel consumption in the country continued to grow, new investments started pouring into the industry
through strong initiatives of private entrepreneurs. The public sector also had a major role to play in expanding capacity
mostly through brownfield expansion and modernisation. This strengthened the domestic supply position in the market.
Much of the capacity growth in the industry has been driven by emerging opportunities in the world market. Over the
years, post-reforms, the condition of the market as well as the shape of the industry have changed along with the changes
in the policy environment. The nature of problems has also changed accordingly as the market, earlier driven by
shortages and rationing, came under the pressure of excess production and capacity. The prices dropped in keeping with
international trends, leading to financial distress in the industry. The government, in the face of the emerging crisis in the

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
industry, took steps to pull the industry out of these recessionary conditions by providing protection through tariff and
non-tariff measures.
5.7    The Indian steel industry’s global entry took place at a time when the international market was in turmoil, the
growth prospects were cut short by the rapidly expanding excess capacity in the industry worldwide, slowdown in
demand, massive supply of steel at cut throat prices from the CIS countries and, more so, large restructuring and cost
cutting efforts all over the major steel producing world. This put pressure on the Indian industry that had just added some
state of the art capacities.
5.8    Although the country’s steel exports grew sharply, estimated to touch 3.5 million tons in 2002-03 from about 0.3
million tons in 1991, the growing protectionism worldwide, especially in the developed countries/regions has come as a
major barrier to Indian industry’s globalisation bid. Anti-dumping and countervailing cases against major Indian steel
products like HR coils, plates and CR sheets in the European Union, USA and Canada have significantly reduced the
global opportunities for the Indian steel makers. On top of this, the spate of safeguard measures has also affected, the
interest of the Indian steel industry. As the Indian steel industry faces challenges, there has also been proportionate
protective response from the government in its defence. The import tariff rates have remained at reasonable levels and
anti-dumping actions have been taken on select products.
5.9    The Committee observes that Indian Steel Industry is marching ahead steadily at a pace determined by the process
and forces of liberalisation and globalisation since 1991. Domestic Economic Reforms i.e. de-regulation and removal of
erstwhile licensing system, capital market reforms, full conversion of currency on trade account etc. led to gearing up of
steel industry for its adherence to the guidelines of WTO regime. The globalisation process opened up new opportunities
for Indian steel industry in the world market. The Committee is pleased to note that Indian Steel Industry is undergoing a
sea change to adapt itself as per the requirement of globalised and liberalised economy. However, the Committee is of
the opinion that the Ministry of Steel should undertake steps to mull out the negative impact of liberalisation and
globalisation of Steel industry and accordingly apprise the Committee in its action taken note on the presentation of this
report. Adequate measures may be taken to safeguard the Indian Steel Industry.
6.0    SWOT ANALYSIS OF THE STEEL INDUSTRY
6.1    The Ministry of Steel outline the SWOT Analysis of Indian Steel Industry which is being reproduced as under:-
 Strength  Weaknesses
1. The Indian steel industry has a competitive
advantage on account of (a) low wage rates, 
(b) abundant and low cost supply of iron ore
and (c) superior managerial and technical skill
of the work force.
1. The overall coal and energy costs are higher by global
standards. The high quality coal with low ash (both
coking as well as non-coking) necessary for
metallurgical operations in the steel sector is not
domestically available.
2. The industry has already made inroads into the
world market and is exporting more than 10 per
cent of the output. The product quality from
most of the new generation and modernised
plants has received global acceptance.
2. The labour productivity in the older plants have not 
been up to the mark even though there has been sharp
improvement.
  3. The financial costs are higher due to higher interest
rates and investment cost especially in the new
generation plants. The financial distress in the
industry will come on the way of further growth,
especially for the financially hard-pressed companies.
  4. The plants of SAIL and TISCO are at mid-land
locations and away from the ports as well as from the
major steel consumption centres in the country. This
leads to higher transportation cost making not only
exports uncompetitive but also raise domestic supply
cost.
  5. The overall infrastructure in the country, especially
railways, ports, roadways and power supply are weak
and nowhere near the global standards. This is a big
handicap.

  6. A large segment of the industry, especially the
induction furnaces and re-rolling units, are
excessively fragmented and do not operate under
optimum economies of scale. Even the technology
engaged is outdated leading to higher energy
consumption, waste of input materials and poor
quality of products. A significant quantum of
investment is needed to modernise these sectors.
  7. The steel industry, like most other industries are faced
systemic weaknesses. These raise the transaction costs
for the industry.
 Opportunities  Threats
1. With continuous efforts towards improvement
in product quality, expanding global exposure
and niche product development, the Indian steel
industry has full potential to grow significantly
in the global market. The country is also at an
advantage to cater to the markets in the
neighbourhood (Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and
Nepal importantly), Southeast and East Asia
and the Middle East.
1. Globally, the industry has accumulated huge excess
capacity. This will in the first place keep pressure on
prices and then reduce opportunities for growth. An
international low price syndrome in an era of
liberalisation and globalisation is a major threat for
domestic investment towards capacity growth.
2. India is a large and growing economy. The
domestic market advantage is significant
compared to many other steel producing
countries where domestic steel demand has
stopped growing.
2. Given the poor state of health of the steel industry in
India, a sustained period of low international prices
may lead the industry to bankruptcy unless available
policy tools adequately protect them.
3. Adaptability to small batch production will
provide opportunities for niche
products.                           
3. Protectionism has grown worldwide and major Indian
steel products are under trade actions in
countries/regions like the USA, EU, Canada,
Thailand, etc.
  4. Stricter subsidy disciplines may adversely affect the
Indian steel industry’s margins as well as its exports.
  5. Poor infrastructure in the country may add to the costs
of production further making exports unviable in this
strongly competitive world market.
6.2    The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should have the objective assessment of SWOT analysis for
improving the health of Indian Steel industry. Since the SWOT analysis gives the details of the strength, weaknesses,
opportunities and threats to the objects undertaken, it is imperative that the strength is the subject where the strategy-
maker has to bank on, while, weaknesses are to be overcome. Similarly, opportunities are to be availed of and a resilient
strategy has to be sketched up for combating the threats coming across. In this context the Indian Steel Industry policy-
maker has to bank on the low wage rates, low iron cost, superior managerial skill while searching for an adequate
marketing strategy. Further avenues may be opened up for supplying semi-steel products to small scale steel industries
and ancillary steel industries in various parts of country (especially Chennai and Ludhiana where clusters of steel units
are wide spread).

Limited (SAIL). The sustainability of BRL’s operations is based both on the inherent strengths that the company

areas, Availability of skilled manpower in the company, Proven quality of the products manufactured by BRL,
Locational advantages derived from being situated close to all the steel plants of SAIL, Technological tie-up with
refractory majors of Japan which has invested the company with a technological edge over other refractory
manufacturers.

13.5  The Techno-Economic Viability (TEV) study was conducted by MECON Limited on the orders of BIFR. The
study has concluded that the company could be revived if certain measures were undertaken by the company and the
Government for the revival of the company. Accordingly, the Government has approved a package for the revival of the
company in June, 2002. The main elements of the revival package are as follows:-
         (i)     Rs. 55.00 Crs. as Non-Plan Loan Assistance to liquidate statutory dues in respect of employees who have
either already accepted VRS/Superannuated or are likely to accept VRS with normal rate of interest.
         (ii)     Rs. 90.00 Crores as Non-Plan Loan for implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme to bring down the

         (iii)    Govt. Guarantee (without any guarantee fee) for raising Rs. 30 Crores for meeting Working Capital

         (v)    Conversion of existing Plan & Non Plan Loans as on 2000-01 amounting to Rs. 97.89 crores into equity.
         (vi)    Moratorium on the repayment of loans and interest up to 2010-2011.

         (ii)     Infusion of funds for working capital and AMR will improve capacity utilization and enable it to execute

funds for AMR.
         (iii)    The adoption of a product mix as suggested in the TEV study will reduce cost of production as also enable it

         (iv)    Revival measures such as conversion of loan into equity, holiday from interest payments and moratorium on

         (v)    Fulfillment of critical assumptions such as implementation of plans for diversification, plans for starting

increase in turnover and profit margins.

14.6  During the past few years performance of SAIL has been affected mainly due to general shutdown in the economy,
fall in international prices, oversupply situation in the domestic market etc.   However, performance has shown
considerable improvement during the current year (2002-03) upto December, 2002 and losses have come down by 57%
over corresponding period last year.
14.7  SAIL has been taking number of steps on continuous basis to improve performance which inter-alia include:
         (i)     Business restructuring envisaging divestment of non-core assets
         (ii)     Intensive cost control
         (iii)    Control on capital expenditure
         (iv)    Market oriented product-mix, reinforcing sales and marketing efforts, greater focus on customer satisfaction.
         (v)    Rightsizing of Manpower
         (vi)    Reduction in borrowings
14.8  The Committee notes the steps taken by SAIL management for improving the financial position of SAIL and hopes
that the steps so undertaken would lead to emancipation of SAIL from deeply rooted financial problem. The Committee
hopes that with the upswing of Steel Industry in general SAIL would turn around for saving its status of Nav-ratna. The
Committee hopes that SAIL would adhere to its time frame as set in MoU target for rationalization of man power.

20.19  I would like to explain what exactly we have done. In the case of our production this year, we have achieved a
record production in the saleable steel. It is more than 10 million tones, with a growth rate of 7%. In crude steel
production, we have achieved a growth rate of 6 per cent over the previous year. The plants are now operating at almost
100 per cent capacity utilization. The production has been very good.
20.20  So far as sales are concerned, we have seen a growth in our sales by about ten per cent on an average. The export
growth has been about 55 per cent in the current year. This year, we are glad to have export of about 7000 k tones. About
prices also, on an average, we are seeing price improvement by about 16 per cent. Our market today is very closely
linked with the international market. If the international market goes up, we have the impact on our scenario also. On an
average, we had about 16 to 17 per cent improvement in the flat products. In the case of long product, it was much less,
but it is emerging now. Manpower has been area of concern. We have been working out manpower rationalization. As of
March, 1998, we have been able to reduce our manpower by 40,000. Even in the current year, we have been able to do it,
and we have done it with the help of VRS. We have been working very hard on cost control measures. Sir, I am also glad
to inform that there was a lot of apprehension and worry on account of modernization of our Durgapur, Rourkela and
Bokaro steel plants. We spent almost about Rs.12,000 crores on modernization, and a bulk of this amount had to be
borrowed from the market to finance these schemes. As a result, our debt burden has gone up quite heavily. In the
current year, we have been able to reduce our borrowings. We have been able to negotiate with the bankers a substitution
of interest rate and on an average about one-and-a-half per cent deduction in the overall interest rate has also been
achieved in the current year. We have effected a saving of about Rs.250 crores on interest burden alone, and a reduction
in the total borrowings amounting to Rs.700 to Rs.750 crores. About the modernization of the Durgapur steel plant, we
have had 90 per cent capacity utilization in the saleable steel. Energy consumption went up from 1.7GW to 7.3GW. So,
physical parameters in the case of the Durgapur steel plant have been virtually achieved. It is now in the zone of just

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
breaking even. If we take into account the monthly figures of February and March, it is in the breakeven zone, and
interestingly, this is happening after a gap of about 22 years. Similarly, in the case of Rourkela also, there has been a
very sharp and considerable improvement. The production has improved by about 13 per cent, and the Rourkela plant is
also making cash profit, and we are sure, the way things are going, very progressing targets have been set for the next
year, towards the end of the next financial year, Rourkela could also enter the zone of break-even. Bhilai and Bokaro are
already profit-making units. In the case of Bhilai plant, the rolled metal supply has been in the range of about 600 to 700
MT. This is a record. It is one of the best in the world. There has been an absolutely total acceptability of the system. On
production front, sales front, controlling of capital expenditure, borrowing costs, manpower rationalization, things are all
under control and in the next year, we are very confident that we should be able to really turn around the company and
make profit. In fact, in the MoU that we have submitted, we have projected profit in the next year.”
20.21  Till recently, the Committee was of the opinion that SAIL suffered losses and was in deep trouble when SAIL was
failing in generating extra budgetary internal resources as per the set target as a result of which capital projects/schemes
get either scuttled or delayed. The Committee felt in its 70 th report on Demand for Grants 2002-03 that the status of
‘Nav-Ratan’ was at stake if the proposed business and financial restructuring of SAIL could not fructify in time, the
Committee had fears about the possibility of sinking of SAIL and wanted to call the immediate attention of Government
to this.
20.22  The un-audited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a sharp improvement in the
performance with losses being slashed to Rs.79 crore in Q3 ’02 – an improvement of Rs. 507 crore over the
corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December ’02 was brought to a level of Rs. 558 crore,
showing a recovery of 57 percent over the results of the same period in 2001 which helped the company to post a cash
profit of Rs. 215 crore in Q3’02 as against a loss of Rs. 297 crore in Q3’01 and a cash profit of Rs. 305 crore in the first
nine months of the current financial year. SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs. 434 crore during the corresponding period
in the last fiscal year. SAIL offered a loss of whopping  Rs. 1707.00 crore during 2001-02. Among SAIL PSUs only BSP
is doing well and DSP is trying to catch up with the stabilization of modernisation programmes. Performance of RSP
continues to be miserable. Due to the improved performance of steel companies during the current financial year on
account of good demand and higher price realization, SAIL shares started to lock up and in January 2003 it crossed its
par value. Investors’ mood is gradually gaining confidence as SAIL issue price has started to mounting up, hovering
around Rs. 9-9.25. However, the debt instrument of SAIL has been rated by CRISIL as inadequate safety for fixed
deposit programme and Bond programme. The debt-equity ratio stands at 5.52:1 as on 31.12.2001 and SAIL is trying to
coming out of woods.                       
21.0    FINANCIAL RESTRUCTURING PACKAGE OF SAIL
21.1    The financial restructuring package of SAIL has been completed. For the business restructuring, most of the tasks
have been completed. However, there is a delay in divestment of non-core assets as well as in the reduction in the total
number of employees of SAIL. The status of the divestment of non-core assets (Asset Restructuring/Divestments) as on
12.03.2003 is as follows:---
21.2    Divestment of Oxygen Plant-2 of Bhilai Steel Plant (BSP) : In the first round of divestment, no meeting point
could be reached with the highest bidder. As advised by SAIL Board, fresh Expression of Interest (EOI) was invited on a
global basis through a press advertisement in May 2002 with relaxed eligibility criteria. Two parties have submitted their
EOIs, and the process is continuing.
21.3    Divestment of Visvesvaraya Iron & Steel Plant (VISP) : Based on the report submitted by Industrial Development
Bank of India (IDBI), Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL) has decided that :
     (a)  The divestment process of VISP may be treated as closed.
     (b)  The performance of VISP will be observed for the next six months.
     (c)  In case there is no improvement, a view may be taken regarding suspension of operations.
     (d)  Within 1-2 years fresh efforts for divestment can be made.
21.4    Divestment of Alloy Steel Plant (ASP) : In view of the fact that divestment of ASP has been taken as closed, it has
been decided not to pursue the divestment option for the time being. The task is, therefore, being treated as closed for the
present.
21.4.1 Following strategy for reducing loss is being followed in the mean time :
     (a)  Major thrust on manpower reduction
     (b)  Control of operation based on market and financial considerations.
     (c)  Thrust on cost reduction

     (d)  Transfer of steel from Durgapur Steel Plant
     (e)  Improving operational efficiency & utilising ASP-SSP synergy for short term gain.
21.4.2 This may reduce the losses to about Rs. 5-6 crores/month, but will not turnaround ASP.
21.5    Divestment of Salem Steel Plant (SSP) : the party has submitted Price bid and the bid is in the process of being
evaluated.
21.6    Divestment of Rourkela Fertilizer Plant (RFP) : Based on discussions with the shortlisted parties, it has been
decided to ask for fresh bids to a modified proposal from the two shortlisted parties. Further, SAIL is working out
financial implications, if any, of the transfer of land to a joint venture company.
21.7    Disinvestment of IISCO : The disinvestment process has been suspended as no response has been received from
M/s. TPE, the only party in the fray. SAIL is currently pursuing the rehabilitation proposal approved by Govt. of India
for final clearance by IDBI/BIFR. In the hearing held on 14.2.03, the Bench of BIFR has granted 6 weeks time to IDBI
(Operating Agency) to submit a status report alongwith a Draft Rehabilitation Scheme for IISCO. Meanwhile, as a part
of rehabilitation proposal, a VRS has been launched at Kulti Works. Fresh efforts for disinvestments may be initiated
later depending upon market condition and IISCO’s rehabilitation position.
22.0    ORGANISATION RESTRUCTURING IN SAIL
22.1    Rightsizing manpower : Substantial progress has been made in rightsizing manpower and this is a continuous
thrust area. SAIL had reduced its manpower since 1999-2000 by around 34000 (reduction is about 50,000 since 1996-
97). The manpower of SAIL as on 28.02.03 is 1,37,947 (excluding subsidiaries). In the current VRS-II 2002, around
1657 applications have been approved. In VRS-I 2002, 3858 people has been separated. Around 10,000 separations are
expected in the current year, out of which separations against VR would be around 5500. The VR scheme has been
extended upto March, 2003. However, it may be mentioned that response to VR is on the decline, especially with recent
improvement in the financials of SAIL. The reduction of around 10,000 persons per year have been achieved in last four
years and if this rate is maintained the manpower may get reduced to a level of about 1,00,000 in a period of 3-4 years
from now.
22.2    Strategic Business Unit (SBU)
22.2.1 Product based SBU structure was proposed with the basic objective of giving thrust to product based marketing
and to integrate production with marketing. All the changes required at the operating level have been implemented i.e.
product-based marketing has been implemented; and two separate groups are handling marketing of longs and flat
products. The marketing and warehouse functions have been separated with stockyards getting separated from branches.
With the implementation of KAM process, integration between production and marketing has improved.
22.2.2 The stage-2 of SBU implementation involves board level re-organisation, which may be reviewed after some
time.
22.3    Operation Management
22.3.1 Cost control – Task completed. the cost savings identified in the budget is Rs. 520 crores. Against this target, till
February 2003 a cost reduction savings of around Rs. 375 crores has been achieved.
22.3.2 Sale of Idle Assets – Task completed. Against the target of Rs. 70 crores in 2002-03, sale orders worth Rs. 61
crores have been issued and Rs. 56 crores has been realised through selling of idle assets till  28th February, 2003.
22.3.3 Completed Tasks
           The other MOU tasks which have been completed are divestment of the power plants; Redesigning of the
Incentive Scheme; Redesigning of Key Corporate Process; Improvement in CMO effectiveness; Key Account
Management Process; Incremental Cost Reduction; Purchase Cost Reduction; Selling of idle Assets; effective project
management.
22.4    The Committee, while noting the various aspects and provisions of financial restructuring package of SAIL
consisting of the disinvestments of non-core assets, organizational restructuring (right sizing of man power, strategic
business units operational management i.e. cost control and sale of idle assets) and the details of completed task, hopes
that the timely implementation of financial restructuring package would lead to emancipation of SAIL out of red.

26.2  The Committee hopes that the appropriation of budgetary support of Rs.5.00 crore during 2002-2003, over AMR

modernisation of equipment would further lead to efficient process and mode of production in BRL. Consequent upon
improvement in the production system the physical and the financial performance of the company would automatically
improve.
26.3  Stating the reasons for total obliteration in target set at the BE stage for raising IEBR to the tune of Rs.8.00 crore
during 2002-2003 at RE state and the originally conceived strategy and the schemes which got suffered due to non-
raising of IEBR the ministry of steel stated that the projected IEBR of Rs.8.00 crores during 2002-2003 was based on an
expectation that the revival scheme would be sanctioned in 2000-2001 and implemented in 2002-2003. As this did not
materialise the company was unable to generate any IEBR. As such some plans for AMR will have to be deferred for
subsequent years when Rs.35 crores approved by Government as plan assistance under revival package will become
available.
26.4  As regards the progress made on continuous casting project and the details of feasibility of BRL entering into joint
venture partnership for the purpose it was stated that the Ministry of Steel vide its letter No.4(23)/99-HSM dated
02.09.2002 had specifically desired the Company to implement the project for Continuous Casting Refractories as a part
of diversification programme in line with the TEV Study. Accordingly, the Company approached M/s MECON Ltd. to
update the project cost. M/s MECON Ltd. has updated the project cost to Rs.42.13 crores based on prices prevailing on
the 4th quarter of 2002.
26.5  Further a meeting was held on 3.2.2003 at New Delhi, which was attended by officials of Ministry of Steel, BRL,
MSTC and FSNL, PSUs under Ministry of Steel. The meeting discussed all possible steps for early implementation of
the project with active participation of BRL and MSTC. Since there were conflicting reports in respect of likely demand
for Continuous Casting Refractories it was decided to get a fresh viability report from another consultant. Action in this
regard is being taken. Simultaneously BRL has also entered into negotiations with SAIL for exploring the possibility of
having a MoU with it for SAIL taking 100% of the production of C.C. Refractories from BRL.
26.6  The Committee strongly feels that delay in the sanctioning of the project and its implementation would in no way
emancipate the PSUs but would lead to its further sinking and consequent deterioration in the physical and financial
performance of the company. Therefore, it is suggested that the timely intervention of appropriate technology for
improving the physical performance of the company is the most warranted. The Continuous Casting Project has been
pending since the IX Five Year Plan and the project was deferred for the X Five Year Plan on the plea of Market
Demand scenario of refractories and unsound financial performance of the company. At a time when the revival package
has been sanctioned for BRL it is not prudent to defer the implementation of continuous casting project. Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should act promptly in removing the initial loggerheads on way to the
implementation of the project. The Ministry of Steel may constitute a Task Force of the expert for the viability of the
project and its opinion could be obtained within 30 days of its constitution as postponing the project on one or another
plea would not only hamper the financial performance of the company but it would also mar the prospects of the success
of the revival package sanctioned for BRL.

36.0  IMPACT OF RATIONALIZATION OF TAX STRUCTURE MADE IN BUDGET 2002-2003 ON THE

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
INDIAN STEEL
36.1  The General Budget for 2003-2004 has provided a thrust to infrastructure projects such as roads, airports, and
seaports through an innovative funding mechanism which prove helpful to the domestic steel industry by boosting the
demand for steel in the country. As regards the impact of rationalization of tax structure, made in budget, on the steel
sector and further tax reforms that may be suggested, a detailed note is given in the subsequent paragraphs.
36.2  Impact of rationalization of tax structure : The Union Budget 2003-2004 has increased Customs Duty on charge
Nickel and Metcoke from 5% to 10% in pursuance of government’s policy to minimize sector-specific and end-use based
customs duty.
36.3  Nickel :- In the case of Nickel, some of the end-users were paying duty at the rate of 15% and others were paying
5%. However, the predominant import of nickel [approx. 30,000 MT out of total imports of 34,000] is for manufacture of
stainless steel and only a minscule proportion of the users (primarily plating industry) were actually paying the higher
duty of 15%. If rationalization had to be done, the duty could have been fixed at 5% for all users keeping in view the
dominant user industry. Moreover, Nickel is not produced in this country at all. Therefore, there is no domestic industry,
which competes with imports. Further, the predominant usage of stainless steel in India is for the utensil sector. The
utensil sector has been encouraged by the Government as reflected in the excise duty exemption to the utensil
manufacturers announced in the Budget. However, the benefit of the excise duty exemption may be eroded by doubling
of customs duty rate on nickel contributes 
50-60% of the total cost of stainless steel and is thus the single most dominant raw material in stainless steel. Moreover,
the international price of nickel has risen from $6000/MT to over $9000/MT over the last one year and the increase in
customs duty adds to the increased cost being borne by manufacturers of Stainless Steel.
36.4  Metcoke :- The customs duty on Metcoke has also been rationalized to a uniform rate of 10%. This too appears to
have been done in pursuance of the policy to minimize sector-specific and end-use based customs duty
variations/exemptions. The steel industry as well as the ferro alloy industry are both going to be adversely affected since
they have been paying a 5% duty on imported Metcoke. The import duty for steel/pig-iron industry using blast furnace
technology was reduced from 15% to 5% in the year 2000 after protracted correspondence with Ministry of Finance. The
benefit was extended to steel manufacturers using COREX Technology in the Budget 2002-2003 and to the Ferro Alloy
Industry as late as in January 2003.
36.4.1  The grounds on which Ministry of Steel had recommended reduction in the import duty on Metcoke for the steel
industry and the Ferro Alloy Industry still holds true. The Mini Blast Furnace Units as well as the Ferro Alloy industry
requires Low Ash Metcoke (LAM), the indigenous availability of which is limited. Therefore, the requirement of LAM
by both these industries is almost entirely met through imports from China.
36.4.2  Though the indigenous Metcoke industry needs to be encouraged, it cannot be given protection at the cost of
Steel/Ferro Alloy industry, especially when the required quality of Metcoke is not available in the country. In fact
Ministry of Steel has been proposing that a different (rate of)’’ in the import duty between Coking Coal-the raw material
for production of Metcoke, and Metcoke should be maintained by reducing the duty on Coking Coal to 0% and retaining
the duty of 5% on Metcoke.
36.4.3  The logic of minimizing sector-specific and end-use based customs duty exemptions/reductions may not be
applicable in this case. Around 29 lac tons of Metcoke is imported every year out of which more than three quarter is
consumed by the steel industry and the remaining mainly be the Ferro Alloy and the Chemical industry. Therefore, in
this case also the rationalization in customs duty could have been done keeping in view the interest of the dominant user
industries i.e. the Steel and the Ferro Alloy industry. Further, as in the case of Nickel, the international price of LAM has
risen by more than 50% over the last one year.
36.5     Excise Duty on stockyard and freight charges :- Ministry of Steel had sought that stand-alone secondary
producers and integrated steel plants (ISP) be treated at par and excise duty be levied on the basis price alone, a facility
available till now only with the ISPs. However, the Budget 2003-2004 has withdrawn the facility given to ISPs and they
would now have to pay excise duty on normal transaction value at depots. This would imply that stockyard price for non-
modvatable items like plates etc. would go up by an average of Rs.150-200 per ton.
36.5.1  ISPs like SAIL established a stockyard network across the length and breadth of the country in order to reach
steel to the common man and also to rural and backward areas. However, owing to levy of excise duty on freight and
distribution charges, the steel will become costlier for deliveries from stockyards. The small-scale
manufacturers/consumers requiring steel in small quantities and who are unable to procure rake-roads directly from the
plants will be put to disadvantage.
36.5.2  In addition, the viability of the stockyards would itself get affected since steel sold through them would get
costlier, vis-a-vis traders who might procure steel directly from ISPs and would not have to pay excise duty on freight,
though final destination for both could be the same. Therefore, this Ministry is of the view that, stand-alone secondary
producers and integrated steel plants (ISP) should be treated at par and excise duty levied on the basic price along.

36.6     Tax Reforms :- The Ministry of Steel suggested the Ministry of Finance to address the adverse impact of tax
proposals on the steel industry by amending the tax proposals.
36.7     Customs Duty
36.7.1  Duty on Coin Blanks :- The import of Coin Blank is duty free. This puts the domestic Coin Blanks manufacturers
at a disadvantage since they have to pay sales tax and other transaction charges. In order to provide an even playing field
to the domestic industry it was proposed by Ministry of Steel that a customs duty of 30%, which is the same as the duty
on Cold Rolled Stainless Steel, (CRSS is the input for the manufacture of Coin Blanks) should be imposed on imported
Coin Blanks alongwith 4% SAD and 16% CVED. Alternately, deemed export benefits should be extended to the supply
of Ferritic Stainless Steel Coil Blanks to the Government of India Mints. In this case, in order to ensure a level playing
field with foreign suppliers, it is necessary that domestic suppliers also be provided drawback facility to offset 4% CST
payable.
36.7.2  Withdrawal of SAD from non-available inputs :- In addition to basic customs duty, all imported items (except old
ships) attract 4% SAD, which has been levied to neutralize 4% sales tax on domestic sales. From 1999, traders have also
been brought under SAD. However, to enable import of essential raw materials, SAD should be waived on items, which
are not available indigenously. A list of such items along with their custom tariff numbers is given in the table below :

36.7.4 Hot Rolled Stainless Steel Coils (HRSS) for Coin-Blanks :- HRSS imported for manufacture of Coin Blanks for

metric ton of Coin Blanks as approved by the government is 1.8654 metric on whereas the exemption is available only

should be given against manufacture of every ton of Coin Blank.

of 16% on import of old ships for breaking so that (a) tax evasion is reduced and revenue collection is increased and (b)
the industry gets the requisite boost in production.
36.8    Excise Duty
36.8.1 Reduction of excise duty on GP/GC sheets for rural/mass consumption :-
           One of the constraints in growth of domestic demand for steel is the high excise duty of 16%. Whereas
intermediate consumers such as machinery manufacturers can adjust the excise duty paid on steel inputs by way of
paying only CENVAT at the time of sales of their products, final consumers such as house builders, construction

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
industry etc. have to bear the burden of excise duty. The situation is more alarming in the rural sector that consumes
large quantities of GP/GC sheets. In order to boost market demand of steel it is necessary to reduce the cost of
production as well as the market price of iron and steel products. In view of this the excise duty on GP/GC sheets should
be reduced from 16% to 8%. Apparently this may cause loss of revenue, but with production going up such loss will be
compensated.
36.8.2  Notification 345 dated. 23.10.97 regarding clearance of recoveries on ship breaking:-
           A section of the steel industry as well as ship-breakers have drawn our attention to provisions laid down in
Notification No. 345/61/97-CX dated 23.10.97. This notification clarifies that no central excise duty is payable on goods
and materials (recovered during the course of ship-breaking) which are outside the ambit of Section XV of the Schedule
to the CE tariff Act, 1985 and no reversal of MODVAT credit taken on input of entire ship is warranted in respect of
such recovered goods which are considered as not arising out of an activity of manufacture or processing. However, this
provision is being misused by excessive billing of non-excisable goods like generators, motors etc. and temptation for
ship-breakers for selling the same to scrap traders without payment of excise duty, thereby violating the norm of value
addition through breaking of a ship. This notification is giving an undue advantage to unscrupulous ship-breakers. It
would have been logical to charge ED on their sales also after recovery as scrap items from the ships. Therefore the
above CE Notification should be withdrawn. At the same time, non-excisable items such as generators, refrigerators etc.
which are a part of the imported ship, should also be charged customs duty under their respective heading as is being
done in case of bunk oil.
36.8.3 Excise Duty on pre fabricated items of steel used in construction:
           Both steel and cement are used for construction. Items fabricated both out of iron & steel (CH.7308.50) and
cement (CH.38) at the project site continue to be exempt from duty. However, while the prefabricated cement items
(ready mix concrete: CH 3824.20) are exempt from payment of excise duty, prefabricated steel items attract an Excise
Duty of 16%. Since steel and cement both are extensively used in construction prefabricated steel structure (73.08) and
prefabricated buildings (94.06) should be exempted from Excise Duty.
36.9  After having a detailed discussion with the representatives of Indian Steel Alliance, TISCO, Jindal Vijay Nagar the
Committee feels that the existing tax structure needs to be modified to become a source of support for the steel sector.
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Finance should examine the issue of rationalizing the tax structure on
the following lines :-
         (i)     Customs duty on charge nickel and Metcoke be fixed at 5% for all uses keeping in view the dominant user
industry. The Committee agrees with the proposal of the Ministry of Mines that a differential of in the import
duty between Coking Coal – the raw material for production of Metcoke, and Metcoke should be maintained
by reducing the duty on Coking Coal to 0% and retaining the duty of 5% on Metcoke.
         (ii)     Prior to the budget 2003-2004 integrated steel manufacturers were paying Excise duty on the factory gate,
even when goods were sold from the stockyard. It is now proposed that Excise duty has to be paid on
transaction value at depot. Withdrawal of the existing facility would imply an increase in price of construction
steel in particular for supply from stockyard, affecting SAIL and TISCO specifically. Reinstatement of the
existing notification is required.
         (iii)     While there is an exemption of customs duty on Stainless Steel coin blanks, domestic manufacturers such as
SAIL and other have to pay excise duty and local taxes on similar products made in India. This product is
bought by the Ministry of Finance only. Indian companies are loosing tenders to overseas companies. The
Department of Economic affairs must allow exemption of excise duty and sales tax for local producers
supplying to them.
         (iv)    Restoration of status quo ante i.e. 5% import duty, 4% SAD and CVED of 16% on import of old ships for
breaking so that (a) tax evasion is reduced and revenue collection is increased and (b) the industry gets the
requisite boost in production.
         (v)    Reduction of excise duty on GP/GC sheets from 16% to 8% for promoting rural mass consumption.
         (vi)    Withdrawal of Notification 345 dated 23.10.97 regarding clearance of recoveries on ship-breaking and
charging of custom duty on non-excisable items like generators, refrigerators, under their respective heading
as is being done in case of bunk oil.
         (vii)   Exemption of excise duty on prefabricated item of steel used in construction in line with exemption of excise
